Use this approach when the output can be checked objectively: file transforms, extraction, generated code, fixed steps. Writing style and coaching cannot be graded well, so those skills do better with lean and a trigger eval.

## Skill-Creator Loop

This is the loop from Anthropic's skill-creator, using BMad's shapes and eval runner. Smithy writes a draft with a deliberately specific description, because widening a description is easier than narrowing it. It writes two or three prompts with empty rubrics, then runs the loop. After that, `bmad-eval` tunes the description, and Smithy asks whether a team needs to change a rule or step without forking.

If you have a skill-creator `evals.json`, `bmad-eval` can convert it.

## The Eval Loop

Eval-first and the skill-creator loop share one loop. Each round does the following:

1. Run the skill and the bare model on the same inputs.
2. Write the rubric from the first outputs, one binary check per failure seen. Drop a check that passes in both arms, because it tests nothing the skill adds.
3. Grade three runs per case and read the difference between the arms.
4. Read the transcripts as well as the grades.
5. Change one thing, and cut any line whose removal did not change results.
6. Rerun against the prior version to see whether the change moved the score.

The loop stops when every check passes on three runs, or when you say it is good enough. If two rounds move nothing, the cases are the problem. If the skill stays behind the bare model, the model has caught up, and Smithy proposes retiring the skill.

## From Session Logs

Use menu code `LOGS`, or say "make a skill from my sessions". This approach starts before discovery.

Smithy offers to read the logs of the agent you are talking to, your memlogs, or files you name. It confirms the location with you, or asks if it cannot find it, and waits for a yes before reading.

It then proposes at most three candidates. Each is a repeated request with its counts: how often you asked, in which words, which tools ran in which order, and your corrections word for word. Your corrections are the know-how a skill encodes. A request you never corrected is probably one the model already does well.

When your corrections show an installed skill falling short, and that skill has a `customize.toml`, the candidate is a customization of it, not a new skill. It goes to `bmad-customize`. For a new skill, you pick one candidate and discovery asks only what the logs cannot say. The build then runs the lean way.

:::tip[Keep repeating yourself?]
You do not need logs to capture something you do by hand. Say "turn this chat into a skill" or "I keep pasting this prompt", and Smithy mines the conversation first.
:::
docs/toolsmith/bmad-eval.md:
---
title: 'Eval Runner'
description: 'Measure whether a skill works with bmad-eval: baseline, variant, quality, and trigger runs in a clean working directory, with a permanent record of each run.'
sidebar:
  order: 13
---

`bmad-eval` runs a skill through your own coding tool in a clean working directory and reports what came back. Use it to find out whether a skill beats the bare model, whether a change helped, whether the output meets a standard, and whether the description fires on the right requests.

Smithy offers an eval at the end of every build and runs `bmad-eval` from its menu, so you will usually reach it there. Call it directly when you have a skill and cases and want the numbers.

## The Four Modes

| Mode | Question it answers | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | Does the skill beat the bare model on the same input? | You want to know whether a skill is worth keeping, or before a release |
| Variant | Does a section earn its place, or does a stripped or prior version do as well? | You cut or changed something and want to know if it mattered |
| Quality | Does the output meet the case's rubric? | You know what good output looks like and want each case graded |
| Trigger | Does the description fire when it should and stay quiet otherwise? | A skill does not fire, fires on the wrong things, or is newly built |

A skill the bare model matches should be retired, not patched. The bare model improves with each release, so a baseline run is worth repeating.

## Run an Eval

Ask for a run in plain words, naming the skill and the mode.

```text
Run a baseline eval on skills/acme-release-notes with 3 runs per case.
```

`bmad-eval` finds the cases in the skill's `evals/` folder, then in `evals/<skill-name>/` under the project. It will not invent cases. It shows a summary before starting: the skill, cases, modes, output folder, and command.

:::caution[Runs bypass permission prompts]
Nobody is there to answer a prompt, so runs turn them off. They are not contained unless the recorded command wraps your tool in a sandbox.
:::

## Write Cases

A case is an input, a rubric, an optional `state_prefix`, and optional fixture files. Cases live in `evals/cases.json`, and [Eval Format](../reference/eval-format.md) has the full format.

- **Use real inputs.** Copy real requests, with their typos and casual wording. A tidy input tests a situation the skill rarely meets.
- **Write rubric entries a wrong output cannot pass.** "`brief.md` exists" passes for an empty file. "`brief.md` names the mid-market insurer segment" does not.
- **Check process as well as output.** A transcript shows which tools ran and in what order. Most of these checks are simple reads, so they need little judgment.
- **Reach mid-workflow turns with a `state_prefix`.** It tells the skill what already happened, so one message can test a clarifying turn or a correction.

Skills that coach or facilitate are hard to grade. Skip the rubric for these and judge the output yourself. A trigger eval still applies.

## How Many Runs

Firing and output are both probabilistic, so one run proves little. Three runs per case is the floor for a settled result, and a result from fewer is reported as a quick look. More runs give a variance figure, or show a difference between two versions. A pass on every run is a pass. A pass on one run in three is a lead to follow.

## Trigger Evals

The description is a skill's only trigger, so a trigger eval runs queries through your real tool and records whether the skill loaded. Each query is marked should-fire or should-not.

The should-not queries matter most when they are near misses: requests that share words and domain with the real ones but belong elsewhere, such as debugging a workflow when the skill builds one. A query that obviously belongs to another skill teaches nothing.

When queries fail, the description is changed in its situations and boundaries, never by pasting in a failed query. `bmad-eval` can also run an optimization loop that improves the description against a held-out test set, so the rewrite does not overfit.

## What Keeps a Run Clean

Each case runs in a temporary folder outside your project, with a copy of the skill and a fresh home folder. Your own skills, memory, settings, and project instructions do not load, unless the recorded `env` or `home_files` bring them in. To test firing, the staged skill asks for a token at the start of the reply, and seeing that token proves the skill loaded on any tool.

Grading is independent too. The grader reads the output, gives no partial credit, puts the burden of proof on a pass, and flags checks that pass for trivial reasons.

## Which Tool Runs It

Evals run through the coding tool you are already using, such as Claude Code or Codex. `bmad-eval` ships no list of tools. The first time it runs in a project, your agent works out four facts about its own tool and proves them on one case:

- The command for one non-interactive run
- The folder it reads skills from
- The environment variables a run needs
- The files that keep it logged in

These are recorded in `bmad-eval`'s customization through `bmad-customize`, where you can read and change them.

## Read the Results

Every run is a timestamped folder in the eval-reports folder inside your output folder. Each case has a subfolder with its prompt, transcript, working directory, and grades. Runs are never deleted or overwritten, so a skill's history stays comparable.

Read the transcripts as well as the grades:

| What you see | What it suggests |
| --- | --- |
| Several approaches before one works | An instruction is too vague |
| An instruction followed where it does not apply | The instruction is too broad |
| Stalling between alternatives | No default was named |
| The same helper rewritten every run | Bundle a script |

Smithy can use these results to improve a skill. See [The Eval Loop](approaches.md#the-eval-loop).
docs/toolsmith/build-your-first-skill.md:
---
title: 'Build Your First Skill'
description: 'Build a skill with Smithy from an idea to a working single-skill module, then add a second skill to make a module.'
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

In this tutorial you build a skill with Smithy, set it up with BMad, and try it on a real request. You then add a second skill, which turns it into a module. The example makes release notes from merged pull requests, but any job you repeat will work.

## What You'll Learn

- How to give Smithy what it needs to build a skill
- How to read and change the execution plan
- What a single-skill module is, and why it is the default
- How to try a skill and test that it fires
- How one skill grows into a module

:::note[Prerequisites]
- BMad installed in your project ([Install BMad](../start/install-bmad.md))
- Toolsmith installed ([Install Toolsmith](toolsmith.md#install-toolsmith))
- A job you have done with an agent more than once
- A real input to try the skill on, such as a recent pull request
:::

:::tip[Quick Path]
Ask Smithy for the skill, answer the gaps, approve the execution plan, then run `bmad setup <code>` and try one real request.
:::

## Understanding What Smithy Builds

Your skill registers with BMad as a module, so `bmad` can set it up, recommend it, and check it for updates. One skill does not need a separate module folder. Its own folder holds everything:

| File | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `SKILL.md` | The description that triggers the skill, and the instructions the agent follows |
| `bmod.toml` | The record that tells `bmad` about the skill |
| `help/help.md` | What the `bmad` skill tells users about the skill |

## Step 1: Say What You Want

Start `bmad-toolsmith` and describe the job in your own words. Include anything you already know.

```text
Build a skill that turns the pull requests merged since the last tag into release notes for our customers.
```

If you have thought it through, say so and Smithy moves straight to confirming what you gave it. If the idea is thin, Smithy pushes back on it before building anything.

## Step 2: Fill the Gaps

Smithy asks only for what your request left out, each question with the answer it would guess, so you can often just confirm. It needs to know:

- What the skill gets done, for whom, and who uses the output
- What must be true of the output for that person to act on it
- The phrases you would type to reach the skill, and nearby requests it should ignore
- Where the know-how lives, such as a runbook, an incident, or your own head
- Whether the output can be checked
- Whether this skill stands alone or more are planned

The question about other skills matters. When more skills are planned, Smithy settles a module code and prefix now, so nothing needs renaming later.

## Step 3: Approve the Execution Plan

Smithy shows what it will build and waits. Read every line, because this is the cheapest moment to change your mind.

:::note[Example]
- **Name:** `acme-release-notes`
- **Purpose:** customer-facing release notes from merged pull requests, for the support team to publish
- **Description:** `Writes customer release notes from merged pull requests. Use when the user says 'write the release notes' or 'what shipped since the last tag'.`
- **Shape:** plain skill
- **Registration:** single-skill module, code `acme`
- **Approach:** lean
- **Location:** the folder your agent reads skills from
:::

Use a prefix of your own, not `bmad-`, which marks skills that BMad ships. A prefix also keeps your skills together in listings.

## Step 4: Let Smithy Build It

After you approve, Smithy writes the skill and shows you the draft and description before going further. When you have a real input, Smithy runs the skill on it once and reads how the run went, then fixes what the run shows.

Five review lenses then read every file. Smithy fixes the defects they find, cuts what a capable model would do unasked, validates the skill, and tells you what changed.

## Step 5: Set Up and Try the Skill

Ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup acme`. Setup registers the module, creates its folder under `_bmad/`, and asks any configuration questions the skill has.

Start a fresh session so your tool loads the new skill, then make a real request with one of your trigger phrases:

```text
Write the release notes for everything since v1.4.0.
```

Check that the skill loaded, and judge the output as the person who will use it. To change something, ask Smithy to edit the skill.

## Step 6: Test That It Fires

Smithy offers a trigger eval at the end of a build. Take it for any skill you expect to fire without being named. Smithy writes queries that should fire the skill and near misses that should not, and `bmad-eval` runs them through your tool. See [Eval Runner](bmad-eval.md).

## Step 7: Add a Second Skill

When a second skill belongs with the first, ask Smithy to build it into the module:

```text
Build acme-release-check for the acme module. It checks that a release branch is ready to tag.
```

The execution plan shows the registration as a member of the module. A single-skill module has no record folder yet, so Smithy moves the record into a new `bmod-acme` folder first. The configuration answers people already gave keep working, because the module code stays the same.

## What You've Accomplished

You built a skill and registered it with BMad, then grew it into a module that `bmad` can set up, recommend, and update.

```text
skills-folder/
├── bmod-acme/                  # the module record
│   ├── SKILL.md                # says only to run bmad setup acme
│   ├── bmod.toml               # code, version, source, members, questions
│   └── help/
│       └── help.md             # what bmad tells users about the module
├── acme-release-notes/
│   ├── SKILL.md
│   └── bmod.toml               # names the record
└── acme-release-check/
    ├── SKILL.md
    └── bmod.toml
```

## Quick Reference

| You want to | Ask |
| --- | --- |
| Build a skill | Smithy, "build a skill that..." |
| Change a skill | Smithy, "change this skill to..." |
| Check it fires | Smithy, "run a trigger eval on this skill" |
| Package finished skills | Smithy, "package these as a module" |
| Set up a module | `bmad`, "bmad setup <code>" |

## Common Questions

- [Do I have to make a module?](#do-i-have-to-make-a-module)
- [What if my project has no `_bmad` folder?](#what-if-my-project-has-no-_bmad-folder)
- [Can I write the skill myself?](#can-i-write-the-skill-myself)
- [Does every job need a skill?](#does-every-job-need-a-skill)

### Do I have to make a module?

No. Tell Smithy you want no record and you get a plain skill. It works the same, but `bmad` does not recommend it, set it up, or check it for updates.

### What if my project has no `_bmad` folder?

Smithy builds a plain skill. You can add a record later through [convert mode](modes.md#convert).

### Can I write the skill myself?

Yes. Use the [scaffold approach](approaches.md#scaffold-and-guide). Smithy lays out the files and leaves the writing to you.

### Does every job need a skill?

No. A job you do once needs no skill. A skill earns its place when it saves you retyping a format, a preference, or a convention, or when it holds know-how the model does not have.

## Getting Help

- Ask the `bmad` skill. It reads Toolsmith's help files and can point you to the right mode.
- Ask in the [BMad Discord](https://discord.gg/gk8jAdXWmj).
- [Open an issue](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/issues) for a bug.

:::tip[Key Takeaways]
- Smithy writes nothing until you approve the execution plan.
- One skill is a single-skill module by default. Say if you want no record.
- Tell Smithy early when more skills are planned, so the name fits the module.
- The description decides whether the skill fires. Test it with a trigger eval.
:::
docs/toolsmith/distribute-your-module.md:
---
title: 'Distribute Your Module'
description: 'Publish a module from a Git repository so others can install it with the Skills CLI, set it up with bmad, and receive updates.'
sidebar:
  order: 11
---

Use Smithy's package mode and a Git repository to publish a module that anyone can add with `npx skills add`. There is no separate registry or build step.

## When to Use This

- You have a skill or module ready to share with a team or the public
- You want `bmad` to check it for updates
- Several projects should use the same version

## When to Skip This

- The skill is for one project. Keep it in that project.
- The skill is not stable yet. Test it locally first.

:::note[Prerequisites]
- A finished skill or set of skills
- A Git repository
- Toolsmith installed
:::

## Steps

### 1. Package the Skills

Ask Smithy to package them. If you built them with Smithy, they are probably registered already. See [Package](modes.md#package).

Smithy asks for the `update_source` if it does not have one. This is where update checks look for your module. Its usual form is `github:<owner>/<repo>/<path>`, where `<path>` is the folder holding your skill folders, such as `skills`. Update checks read `bmod.toml` from the `main` branch. A member's `source` must match its record's `update_source`.

### 2. Lay Out the Repository

Put your skills under `skills/`. A multi-skill module looks like this:

```text
your-repo/
├── skills/
│   ├── bmod-acme/
│   │   ├── SKILL.md
│   │   ├── bmod.toml
│   │   ├── help/
│   │   │   └── help.md
│   │   └── roster.toml
│   ├── acme-release-notes/
│   │   ├── SKILL.md
│   │   └── bmod.toml
│   └── acme-agent-scout/
│       ├── SKILL.md
│       ├── customize.toml
│       └── bmod.toml
├── README.md
└── LICENSE
```

A single-skill module is one folder under `skills/`, with its `help/` folder inside and no `bmod-<code>` folder. A repository can hold several modules. Give each one its own folder, `skills/<code>/`, and point its `update_source` at that folder; then `npx skills add owner/repo/skills/<code>` installs the whole module. `validate_manifests.py` requires all the records in a repository to share one version, and every skill folder to have a `bmod.toml`.

### 3. Validate

Ask Smithy to validate the repository. It runs `validate_manifests.py` and checks each skill. Fix what it reports before you publish. See [Validate](modes.md#validate).

### 4. Test a Local Install

Add the module from its folder in a separate test project, then ask `bmad` to run `bmad setup <code>`. Run `bmad status` to confirm the module and version. Check that its questions read well, and that `bmad` recommends the skills as you intended.

```bash
npx skills add ./path/to/your-repo
```

### 5. Publish

Push to your Git host and tag the release. Tell users how to add the module, and to include the record.

```bash
npx skills add your-org/your-repo
```

Then they ask `bmad` to run `bmad setup acme`. Users can pin to a tag with `your-org/your-repo#v1.2.0`. See [Add Modules](../customize/add-modules.md).

### 6. Ship Updates

- **Bump `version` in the record for every release.** `bmad setup` compares it with the installed version to offer the update.
- **Add new skills to the record's `skills` list.** Add a help entry too, and a roster entry for an agent.
- **Record renames and removals in `retired.toml`.** Setup offers to delete the old skill and moves its custom files to the new name. Never reuse a retired name.
- **Ship a migration when users' files must change.** Add a `migration-<n>.toml` beside `bmod.toml`, and `bmad migrate` will run it.

## What You Get

- A module anyone with access can add with `npx skills add`
- Setup questions asked once per project, with answers kept in the project
- Guidance from the `bmad` skill, based on your help files
- Update checks against your source
- Clean handling of renamed and removed skills

## Tips

- Write a README with what the module does, how to add it, and any outside tools it needs.
- Add a `LICENSE`.
- Use `pre_install_message` for what users must know before an update, and `post_install_message` for what to do after installing.
- Use `required_skills` for a skill your module invokes, with a `source` and a minimum `version` for one from another repository.
- Run a [baseline eval](bmad-eval.md) before you publish. For a distributed skill, only that shows the skill beats the bare model on real cases.
docs/toolsmith/make-a-skill-customizable:
---
title: 'Make a Skill Customizable'
description: 'Use customize.toml to let teams change a skill without forking it: decide what to expose, name it well, wire it into the skill, and test an override.'
sidebar:
  order: 8
---

Use a `customize.toml` to let a team change your skill's behavior without forking it. This page is for authors. To change a skill someone else wrote, see [Customize BMad](../customize/customize-bmad.md).

Every value you expose is a promise. Teams will pin values to it and commit overrides, and later releases must respect it. Expose what really varies between your users, and nothing else.

## When to Use This

- Different teams need different output paths, templates, or rules
- Users would otherwise fork the skill for a small change
- Your skill should run a team's own steps before or after it works

## When to Skip This

- Every user wants roughly the same value. Pick a good default.
- The skill is for you alone.
- The value is the skill's identity, not something it consumes.
- It is a memory agent. Its sanctum is already the place to shape it. See [Agents with Memory](agents-with-memory.md).

:::note[Prerequisites]
- A skill built with Smithy, or a BMad skill of your own
- `bmad-customize` installed, to test an override
:::

## Steps

### 1. Decide What Earns a Setting

Ask three questions of each candidate. Expose it only if it passes all three.

1. Does it really vary across your users?
2. Is it something the skill consumes, such as a template, a fact, or an output path, and not part of what the skill is?
3. Would hiding it force a fork? If one sentence in `persistent_facts` would do, leave it out.

### 2. Ask Smithy to Add It

Tell Smithy during discovery what teams will change, or use [edit mode](modes.md#edit) on a skill you already have. Smithy writes the `customize.toml` and connects each value to the skill.

A skill uses a `[workflow]` table and an agent uses `[agent]`. Do not mix them. Persona fields in `[workflow]` suggest the skill should be an agent.

| Key | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `activation_steps_prepend`, `activation_steps_append` | Steps a team runs before or after activation |
| `persistent_facts` | Standing facts or `file:` globs to load for the run |
| `on_complete` | A hook to run when the skill finishes |
| `<purpose>_output_path` | Where an output lands |
| `run_folder_pattern` | How run folders are named |
| Your own settings | Anything else a team must vary, such as a template path |

### 3. Name Each Setting Clearly

Most users change settings through a conversation with `bmad-customize`, so names should read well aloud. `release_notes_template` works, and `tmpl_override` does not. Comment each one with when to override it.

```toml
[workflow]
# Override to send the notes to your team's release folder.
release_notes_output_path = "{project-root}/docs/releases"

# Override to use your own template.
release_notes_template = "assets/release-notes-template.md"
```

### 4. Set Defaults That Work

The skill must work with no override. Avoid boolean toggles, because a switch usually means the author never decided. Offer a value the skill consumes.

### 5. Read Every Value in the Skill

The skill resolves its table on activation, then reads each value as `{workflow.<key>}` or `{agent.<key>}`.

```bash
uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py --skill {skill-root} --project-root {project-root} --key workflow
```

A value that is declared but hardcoded in the body is a defect, because every override of it does nothing. Smithy's review flags this.

A skill never writes its own overrides, never merges TOML itself, and never carries a second code path for when BMad is absent. `resolve_customization.py` reads, and `bmad-customize` writes. Where users will change a value, the skill says so in one line: invoke `bmad-customize`, naming the key.

### 6. Test an Override

Run `bmad-customize` and change one value. It writes `_bmad/custom/<skill>.toml` for a team or `_bmad/custom/<skill>.user.toml` for one person. Run the skill and confirm the change took effect. [Check what resolved](../customize/customize-bmad.md#check-what-resolved) shows the merged values.

## What You Get

- A `customize.toml` beside `SKILL.md`, holding your defaults and comments
- Overrides that survive updates, because they live in the project and not in the skill
- Layers that merge when the skill activates: scalars override, arrays append, and arrays of tables merge by `code` or `id`

## Tips

- Give each item in an array of tables a `code` or an `id`, or the resolver can only append it.
- Keep project-wide values, such as the output folder, in core config. Read them with `resolve_config.py`.
- For an agent, `name` and `title` are fixed. A team that wants a new name or title creates a new agent.
- When teams differ in which steps run, a [rendered skill](shapes.md#rendered-skill) may fit better.
docs/toolsmith/migrate-an-old-module.md:
---
title: 'Migrate an Old Module'
description: 'Convert a module written for the module.yaml format into a bmod with Smithy.'
sidebar:
  order: 12
---

Use Smithy's migrate mode to convert an old-format module into the current format, in place. A module built before the bmod format carries a setup skill, a `module.yaml`, and a `module-help.csv`, and it does not work with `bmad setup`.

## When to Use This

- Your module has a `<code>-setup` skill, or a `module-setup.md` in a skill's assets
- It carries `module.yaml` and `module-help.csv`
- It writes to `_bmad/config.yaml` or `_bmad/module-help.csv`
- Smithy's validate mode reported it as an old-format module

:::note[Prerequisites]
- The module's source, under version control
- Toolsmith installed
- The module pushed to a Git repository, so you can give its `update_source`
:::

## Steps

### 1. Start the Migration

Ask Smithy to migrate the module, and point at the folder holding its skills and setup skill. For a one-skill module, point at the skill's own folder. Smithy scans the module and asks only for the `update_source`.

### 2. Read the Execution Plan

Smithy shows the whole execution plan as tables and waits for your yes. Nothing changes before that.

| Old | New |
| --- | --- |
| The setup skill and merge scripts | Deleted, with the setup skill listed as removed in `retired.toml` |
| `module.yaml` | `bmod-<code>/bmod.toml`, with one question per config key |
| Agents | `roster.toml` |
| `module-help.csv` | `help/help.md`, with a topic file for a skill that has many rows |
| Each skill | A `bmod.toml` with a `[skill]` table |
| A folder with one skill | A single-skill module, with no `bmod-<code>` folder |

Every config read in the skills changes to use `resolve_config.py`:

- `output_folder` becomes `core.output_folder`.
- A module key becomes `modules.<code>.<key>`. A key that repeats the code must be renamed.
- Reads of `user_name`, `communication_language`, and `document_output_language` are removed, because the current format has no such keys.
- Fallbacks to the old per-module file are removed.

The execution plan also lists what cannot convert:

| Old feature | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Select questions | Become one string, with the options in the prompt, or are dropped |
| Validation, directories, and post-install notes | Have no equivalent, so the skill handles them or they go |
| Headless and inline-argument setup | Removed, because `bmad setup` has neither |
| Answers in `_bmad/config.yaml` | Not carried over, so `bmad setup <code>` asks again |

### 3. Approve

Smithy writes the new files, rewrites each config read, and removes each skill's step that ran the setup skill. It then deletes the listed files and nothing else.

### 4. Review the Checks

Smithy runs the validators on the result and fixes what they find, then finishes with its ship step.

### 5. Run Setup

Ask `bmad` to run `bmad setup <code>`. Answer the questions again, because old answers are not carried over.

## What You Get

- A module that `bmad` can set up, recommend, and update
- Skills that read their configuration through `resolve_config.py`
- A list of what could not convert, so you can decide how to handle it

## Tips

- Commit before you start, so you can read the whole change as a diff.
- Update your README to replace any old install steps with `npx skills add`. See [Distribute Your Module](distribute-your-module.md).
- Check `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` if your repository has one. The current install path does not need it.
docs/toolsmith/modes.md:
---
title: 'Work on an Existing Skill'
description: 'Edit, convert, review, cut, package, validate, and migrate an existing skill or module with Smithy.'
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

Smithy also works on skills that already exist, including ones built elsewhere. Say what you want done, or pick a code from Smithy's menu.

| Mode | Code | What you get | Say |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Edit](#edit) | `EDIT` | One agreed change, with nothing else disturbed | "Change", "fix", "extend", "add a step to" |
| [Convert](#convert) | `CONVERT` | A skill from another tool as a BMad skill | "Convert my Cursor rule", "make this skill work with bmad" |
| [Review](#review) | `REVIEW` | A report of findings, with nothing changed | "Review this skill", "is this any good" |
| [Cut](#cut) | `CUT` | The skill's prose rewritten shorter, uncommitted | "Cut this skill down", "make it smaller" |
| [Package](#package) | `PACKAGE` | One skill or several wrapped as a module | "Package these", "make this a module" |
| [Validate](#validate) | `VALIDATE` | Pass or fail on what would stop it working | "Validate", "check my skill" |
| [Migrate](migrate-an-old-module.md) | `MIGRATE` | An old-format module in the current format | "I have an old module" |

Edit, convert, package, and migrate end with Smithy's ship step: validation, an offered trigger eval, and a hand-off. Convert also runs the review lenses over what Smithy wrote, and the others offer a review. Review and validate write nothing to the skill. Cut runs the validators and leaves the commit to you.

## Edit

Edit changes a skill as you asked and disturbs nothing else. Smithy reads `SKILL.md` and only the files the change touches, then tells you what changes, what stays, and whether the shape or the description changes. A description change is a trigger change, so Smithy says so and extends the trigger queries to cover it.

Smithy waits for your yes, makes the change, and removes any line the change makes dead. If you want to rethink the skill rather than adjust it, Smithy treats that as a new build, using the old skill as input.

## Convert

Convert brings in something from another tool: a skill, a Cursor rule, a GPT, a slash command, or a prompt you keep pasting. Point Smithy at the file, folder, or pasted text. It reads the source whole and takes out the outcome, the consumer, the intended triggers, the know-how a model would not have, and any scripts.

It drops the host tool's mechanics, such as `globs`, `alwaysApply`, `$ARGUMENTS`, and GPT conversation starters. It also drops instructions every model follows unasked. BMad frontmatter is `name` and `description` only.

There are two paths:

- **Rebuilt beside the source.** A new BMad skill in the right shape. Discovery fills what the source never said, usually the consumer, the near misses, and the name. Smithy lists what did not carry over and leaves your source as it was.
- **In place.** Say "make this skill work with bmad". Smithy works in the same folder. It lists what will change first: the name if you want your prefix on it, the description, paths and config reads, what is dropped, and a `bmod.toml` if you want the skill registered.

An outside skill usually gains a description that triggers reliably, paths that work on other machines, configuration read from the project, and registration.

## Review

Review is advice, not a gate. Point Smithy at a skill, whether yours, someone else's, or one you found. A script measures it first: tokens per file and per run, the description, frontmatter, script headers and tests, paths that do not resolve, how it is registered, and paragraphs over 150 words or holding a sentence over 60.

Five lenses then read every file a model would read, each as a separate reader:

| Lens | Looks for |
| --- | --- |
| Architecture | Files, paths, shape, and registration |
| Determinism | What should be a script and what should be prose |
| Leanness | What a capable model would do unasked, duplication, a passage one sentence could replace, paragraphs that mix topics |
| Customization | Declared values that reach nothing, and overrides that cannot land |
| Trigger | The description against the near misses |

Findings appear in chat and in a markdown file in the eval-reports folder, ordered by severity, each with its file and fix. Nothing changes until you choose. Edit mode applies the findings you accept. Cut mode rewrites the whole skill when leanness findings run through it. A variant eval shows whether a proposed cut matters before you make it.

A skill Smithy just built has already been through these lenses. Use review for skills Smithy did not write, or for a second opinion later.

## Cut

The cut mode (menu code `CUT`) rewrites a skill's prose into the fewest words that steer the model as far, without losing a rule. It drops sentences the model does not need, trims the words inside sentences that carry nothing, and recasts a passage that spends lines on a nudge as the few words that give it. There is no percentage to hit: a lean skill comes back nearly unchanged, and a bloated one comes back much shorter. Ask Smithy to "optimize this skill", "cut this skill down" or "make this skill BMad compliant". It is for a skill built elsewhere, or one you want tightened. A skill Smithy builds or converts gets the same treatment before it ships: Smithy applies every finding from its leanness review, then runs the same check for lost rules.

It takes two things:

- The skill to cut.
- Passages to keep word for word: by default each file's frontmatter, which holds the description, an agent's `customize.toml` with its persona, and the parts a rendered skill copies from its shape template, plus any passage, section or decision you name and the `Decision:` lines in the skill's ticket when it has one.

Smithy copies the skill as it stands and counts the tokens in each prompt file, skipping files under about 150 tokens and the protected ones. It removes worked examples first, keeping one only when a one-line format cannot show the same shape. Then one subagent rewrites each file in parallel. A script confirms each file still has every template expression, `{skill-root}` or `{project-root}` path, frontmatter and protected passage it had, and Smithy restores any it lost. A checker compares each file with its old version and lists a loss only when it can name the different action the model would take without the line, and points to passages that fewer words would say as well. Smithy restores those losses and applies the shorter wordings it agrees with. The skill's validation checks run, and the render test for a rendered skill.

Nothing is committed. Smithy shows a table of tokens before and after for each file with the percent saved, the losses it chose not to restore, and the points the cutters were unsure of. You read the diff and commit what you accept. Without subagents, Smithy runs each role itself, one file at a time, and says so.

## Package

Package wraps skills you already have into a module, so `bmad` can set them up, recommend them, and check them for updates. Point Smithy at one skill or a folder of skills. It reads each one and shows one execution plan: the shape, the code, the prefix, the `update_source`, the configuration questions, the roster entries, the help, the dependencies, and the files it will write.

One skill becomes a single-skill module. Two or more become a multi-skill module, and a single-skill module among them keeps its code while its record moves to a `bmod-<code>` folder. A skill that already belongs to another module can be a dependency, not a member.

Smithy offers to add the prefix to a member that lacks it, and says that renaming changes how the skill is invoked. After your yes, it writes the files and changes each skill to read its configuration from `bmad`, replacing each hardcoded value. See [Modules and Registration](modules.md).

## Validate

Validate reports what would stop a skill or module installing, loading, or firing, and it writes nothing. Point it at a skill, a record folder, or a repository. It reports pass or fail, one line per failure with the fix, and whether the target would install and load.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| `validate_manifests.py` | Manifests, membership, versions, retired names, help topics, and the roster, in a repository with `skills/*/bmod.toml` |
| `init_skill.py --check` | Frontmatter, name, description, `[TODO:` markers, and whether `bmod.toml` parses |
| `scan_paths.py` | Paths that do not resolve, bare `scripts/` calls, references into another skill, and old-format names |
| `scan_scripts.py` | Script headers and tests, then runs the skill's tests |

Smithy also judges what the tools cannot, such as a member reading a value no configuration question asks, or a custom skill named `bmad-`. It offers a trigger eval when the skill has `evals/triggers.json`.

An old-format module fails with one line that names [migrate](migrate-an-old-module.md) as the fix.
docs/toolsmith/modules.md:
---
title: 'Modules and Registration'
description: 'What a BMad module is, what registering a skill gives you, the three ways a skill can register, and when to use configuration or customization.'
sidebar:
  order: 10
---

A module is a set of skills that belong together, with a record that tells the `bmad` skill about them. Registering a skill with a module is what lets BMad set it up, recommend it, and check it for updates. This page explains the choices. The exact keys are in [Module Files](../reference/module-files.md).

## What Registering Gives You

| With a record | Without one |
| --- | --- |
| `bmad setup <code>` asks the skill's questions | Setup never sees the skill |
| The `bmad` skill recommends it from help | Help does not know it exists |
| Update checks follow its source | You update it yourself |
| Other skills can require it at a minimum version | Other skills can require it by name only |

A skill with no record still works, and it can still read BMad config and customization.

## Three Ways to Register

Smithy asks whether a skill is part of a module and whether more are planned, then puts the answer in the execution plan.

| Registration | What it is | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-skill module | One folder is both the skill and its record | The default for one skill |
| Member of a module | A small `bmod.toml` names the record, and the record lists the skill | You are building or expanding that module |
| Plain skill | No `bmod.toml` | You want no record, or the project has no `_bmad/` folder |

A planned module of several skills starts as a single-skill module under its code and prefix, so nothing is renamed later. Smithy moves the record to a `bmod-<code>` folder when the second skill arrives, either when you package the skills or when you build the second one into the module. Smithy never writes a record folder for one skill.

A plain skill can register later: [convert mode](modes.md#convert) adds a record to one skill, and [package mode](modes.md#package) wraps several.

## What a Module Holds

**A single-skill module** keeps everything in the skill's folder. Its `bmod.toml` has a `[bmod]` table and an empty `[skill]` table, and a `help/help.md` sits beside it. A skill with nothing to ask has no configuration questions.

**A multi-skill module** has a record folder, `bmod-<code>`, beside the skills it ships.

| In the record | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `SKILL.md` | Tells anyone who opens it to run `bmad setup <code>`, and does nothing else |
| `bmod.toml` | Code, version, source, members, dependencies, questions, and install messages |
| `help/help.md` | What the `bmad` skill reads to guide users, with optional topic files |
| `roster.toml` | The module's agents, so `bmad` and party mode know who is available |
| `retired.toml` | Skills renamed or removed, so setup can clean up |

Each member has its own small `bmod.toml` that names the record and its source, and lists what that skill alone requires. A skill belongs to one module. A skill it uses from another module is a dependency, not a member.

## Name Skills and Modules

Skills carry the module's code as a prefix: `acme-release-notes`, and agents `acme-agent-scout`. `bmad` finds a module by its `[bmod]` table, and validation requires a multi-skill record folder to be `bmod-<code>`. The code is the configuration namespace and what users type in `bmad setup <code>`.

A prefix of your own tells your skills from BMad's, keeps a module's skills together in listings, and lets you group them in traces and usage reports. Reserve `bmad-` for skills shipped by the bmad-code-org. A custom skill named `bmad-` reads as official, and it could collide with a future core skill.

## Configuration or Customization

Modules offer two ways to change behavior, and they answer different questions.

| | Configuration | Customization |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answers | What does this project need to tell the module? | How should this skill behave differently here? |
| Defined in | `[[bmod.config_questions]]` in the record | `customize.toml` in each skill |
| Set by | `bmad setup <code>` | `bmad-customize` |
| Read as | `modules.<code>.<key>` with `resolve_config.py` | `{workflow.<key>}` or `{agent.<key>}` after `resolve_customization.py` |
| Example | A shared path every member reads | An activation step for one skill |

Use a configuration question for a value several skills read the same way. It is asked once, and every member reads the answer. Skip the question when a good default will do, because every question is a cost at setup. See [Make a Skill Customizable](make-a-skill-customizable.md) for the other side.

A `scope = "user"` question is a personal preference and is not committed. A path the team shares stays team scope.

## Write the Help

`help/help.md` has one reader: the `bmad` skill, answering a user. Write what each skill gives, when to recommend it, and what to offer next. Leave out what `bmad` cannot act on, such as install mechanics and manifest keys.

Add a `help/<topic>.md` for depth, and name it in `help.md` with when to read it. A topic that `help.md` does not name is never read.

## Depend on Other Skills

Use `required_skills` for a skill yours invokes, and `recommended_skills` for one that helps beside it. A plain name is a skill from the same source, and a table names one from elsewhere. Module-wide needs go in the record, and one member's needs go in its own file. Smithy asks during a build, and names anything you need to install.

## Add to the BMad Method

Two different things are often called this.

- **Contribute to the method.** Open a pull request to the BMAD-METHOD repository. The skill lives under `skills/method/`, takes a `bmad-` name, and its `bmod.toml` names `bmod-method`.
- **Extend the method in your project.** Make your own module with your own prefix, whose skills require or recommend the method skills they build on. Do not edit the installed method record, because the next update overwrites it.

Build any change to an installed module in its source repository for the same reason.
docs/toolsmith/shapes.md:
---
title: 'Shapes of a Skill'
description: 'The shapes Smithy builds: a plain skill, an agent with capabilities, a memory agent, a rendered skill with customizable steps, a script-backed utility, and single- and multi-skill modules.'
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

A shape is what a skill looks like on disk. Smithy works out the shape from the conversation about purpose, user, and output, and names it in the execution plan with one line on why. You do not need to pick one. If you name a shape up front, Smithy takes it into account and says if the conversation points elsewhere.

| Shape | What you get | Your need lands here when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plain skill | A `SKILL.md`, with references that load only when needed | You want an agent to do one job well on request |
| Agent with capabilities | A named persona with a greeting and a menu | You want someone to work with across turns, who owns related capabilities |
| Memory agent | An agent that keeps a memory folder and wakes as the same self | The agent must build up knowledge across sessions |
| Rendered skill | Steps rendered from switches and prose blocks | Several teams want different steps, and a fork would drift |
| Script-backed utility | A thin `SKILL.md` over tested scripts | Most of the job is mechanical |

Registration is a separate choice. Any of these shapes can stand alone as a single-skill module, join a module, or stay outside the registry. See [Modules and Registration](modules.md).

## Plain Skill

Most needs land here, including long multi-step workflows. A plain skill can hold:

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `SKILL.md` | Frontmatter with `name` and `description`, then the instructions |
| `references/<topic>.md` | A branch that only some runs need, loaded when reached |
| `scripts/<name>.py` | Work with one right answer per input, with a test beside it |
| `assets/` | Templates and files the skill emits |
| `customize.toml` | What a team can change without forking |
| `bmod.toml` | How the skill registers with BMad |

Only `SKILL.md` is required. A skill small enough to be one file is one file. A complex workflow stays a plain skill when each branch sits in its own reference, and it is the right size at any total if one run loads only what it needs.

A BMad skill resolves its configuration through the project's `_bmad/scripts` when it activates. A skill for use outside BMad has no activation section, only plain paths. A skill is one or the other.

## Agent with Capabilities

An agent is a skill named `<prefix>-agent-<name>` with a persona and a menu. Choose an agent when a user will work with it across turns and it owns several related jobs. Choose a plain skill when the job has one output and needs no persona.

The persona lives in an `[agent]` table in `customize.toml`: `name`, `title`, `icon`, `role`, `identity`, `communication_style`, and `principles`. The persona guides the agent when no capability fits, so it is written in the agent's own voice.

Each `[[agent.menu]]` item has a `code`, a `description`, and exactly one of these:

- `skill`, when an installed skill does the job and the agent invokes it.
- `prompt`, holding the whole instruction in a sentence or two, or a line that reads a file under `references/`.

A capability needs its own file only when there is know-how to hold. One big enough to stand alone should become its own skill.

The agent's description lists its name and the phrases of every capability built into it, because nothing else triggers those capabilities. A menu item that runs an installed skill adds no phrases, because that skill triggers itself. In a module, an agent also gets a `roster.toml` entry, which is how `bmad` and party mode know it exists.

## Memory Agent

A memory agent keeps its identity and memory in a project folder and reloads them each session. Build one only when the agent must build up knowledge over time. The test: used daily for a month, would the thirtieth session differ from the first? See [Agents with Memory](agents-with-memory.md).

## Rendered Skill

A rendered skill keeps its steps as a template with switches and prose blocks. Before the skill runs, `render_skill.py` fills the template from the skill's `customize.toml` merged with team and personal overrides, and the agent reads the result. A team can switch off a step, add a rule, or change wording without editing the skill. `bmad-build` is this shape.

It is worth the extra machinery only when teams really differ in which steps run. A skill with one set of steps and a few settable values is a plain skill with a `customize.toml`.

## Script-Backed Utility

A thin `SKILL.md` names the outcome and when to run which script, and tested scripts do the work. It fits jobs with one right answer per input: transforming files, counting, checking structure, and generating from fixed rules. The prose keeps the part that needs judgment, which is what to do with the result. See [Scripts](write-a-good-skill.md#use-scripts-for-work-with-one-right-answer).

## Changing Shape Later

A skill can change shape through [edit mode](modes.md#edit) when its needs grow. Adding a menu to a plain skill or memory to an agent are shape changes, and Smithy says so before making them.
docs/toolsmith/subagent-patterns.md:
---
title: 'Subagent Patterns'
description: 'How a skill can spread its work across subagents to keep the main conversation small, run work in parallel, and get independent judgment.'
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

A subagent is a separate model instance a skill starts for one task. It gets its own context, takes instructions, and returns a result. Use subagents to keep the main conversation small, to run work in parallel, or to get judgment that the rest of the session has not influenced.

Smithy uses them this way: review sends each lens to its own reader, and cut gives each file its own writer and a separate checker.

## Keep the Parent from Reading First

This is the most common failure. If the parent reads every file before starting subagents, the tokens are already spent, and the main reason for the pattern is gone. It happens easily, because a helpful parent reads ahead.

Say in the skill what the parent does and does not do:

| Tell the parent | Example wording |
| --- | --- |
| What to discover, not read | "List the files in `references/` to decide how many subagents to start. Do not read them." |
| What each subagent returns | "Return only findings about the topic, as JSON at the given path. Do not echo the source." |
| Where its role ends | "You orchestrate. Scripts and subagents do the analysis." |

A pre-pass script helps here. It gives the parent file names, sizes, and structure, so it can plan without reading anything. Run the skill and watch what the parent does, then tighten the wording if it reads ahead.

## Use Files as Shared State

Subagents share nothing but what you give them, so use files to pass work between them. The parent holds file paths and a plan, not the data. Each subagent reads the files it was given and writes a result to a known path, in a strict format the parent can parse.

## Patterns

| Pattern | How it works | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delegated reading | Subagents each read a source and return a short summary. The parent works from the summaries. | There are many documents to read. It is not worth it for one or two files. |
| Temp file assembly | Workers write results to temp files, and a separate subagent combines them. | Summaries are still too large to return, or assembly needs a fresh context. |
| Shared file pipeline | Each subagent reads a shared file and adds to it, in an order the parent controls. | Later work depends on earlier work. |
| Lead and workers | A lead subagent analyzes the task and writes a plan, and the parent starts workers from it. | The work cannot be divided until someone has analyzed it. |
| Parallel perspectives | Subagents with different personas work alone, and an evaluator merges the best of each. | Different perspectives improve quality, as in design decisions and reviews. |
| Generate and select | Many agents try variations, an evaluator scores them, and the next round starts from the winners. | You can score results, and many rounds are affordable. |

Patterns combine. A review might use delegated reading to gather facts, parallel perspectives to judge them, and temp file assembly for the report.

## Make Perspectives Independent

Parallel reviewers only help if they judge independently. Give each one the material and a strong persona or lens, not your conclusion. A reviewer handed your opinion tends to confirm it. Useful perspectives include an architect, someone trying to break the work, a pragmatist asking what the minimum is, and an advocate for the end user.

## Always Provide a Fallback

Skills run on tools and models that may not offer subagents. A skill that fails without them is fragile. Say what happens instead, usually running each role inline one at a time, and have the skill tell the user it did so. Smithy works this way in both review and cut.

:::tip[Start small]
Start with one parent and a first wave of subagents, and add structure only when a run shows the need. Use separate folders or worktrees when parallel agents write files, so they cannot overwrite each other.
:::
docs/toolsmith/toolsmith.md:
---
title: 'Toolsmith'
description: 'What the Toolsmith module is: one agent, Smithy, that builds skills, agents, and modules for BMad, and an eval runner beside it.'
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

Toolsmith is the module for authoring BMad content. Its agent, Smithy (`bmad-toolsmith`), builds a skill, an agent, or a module from a conversation about what you need. `bmad-eval` measures whether a skill works. Use Toolsmith when you want an agent to do a job the same way every time, and when you want to share that job with a team or publish it.

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. Your coding tool reads the description in that file to decide when to load the skill, and the agent follows the rest of the file once it does. Everything Toolsmith builds starts from that folder.

## Install Toolsmith

Toolsmith installs from the BMAD-METHOD repository. If you do not have BMad yet, start with [Install BMad](../start/install-bmad.md). Then add the module from your project folder:

```bash
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/toolsmith --skill '*'
```

Ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup toolsmith`. The module asks no setup questions.

## Talk to Smithy

Start the `bmad-toolsmith` skill, or ask for Smithy by name, and say what you want. You do not need to know the shape of the result, or which mode to use. Smithy shows a menu when you give no request.

| Code | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `BUILD` | Build a new skill, agent, or module from a conversation |
| `SCAFFOLD` | Lay out a skill you will write yourself |
| `LOGS` | Propose a skill from your session logs, then build it |
| `EDIT` | Change, fix, or extend a skill |
| `CONVERT` | Rebuild a skill, prompt, or command from another tool as a BMad skill |
| `REVIEW` | Review a skill and write a report of findings |
| `CUT` | Cut a skill's prose to what changes what the model does |
| `PACKAGE` | Package one skill or several into a module |
| `VALIDATE` | Check a skill or module for what would stop it installing, loading, or firing |
| `MIGRATE` | Convert an old-format module to the current format |
| `EVAL` | Run, benchmark, or trigger-test a skill with `bmad-eval` |

## How a Build Works

Every new skill follows the same path. If you use the scaffold approach to write the skill yourself, steps 3 and 4 are yours.

1. **Discovery.** Smithy reads what you have already said and asks only for what is missing, one or two questions at a time.
2. **Smithy execution plan.** Smithy shows the name, purpose, description, shape, registration, approach, location, and files. Nothing is written until you approve it, and you can change any line.
3. **Build.** Smithy writes the skill, and tries it on a real input when you have one.
4. **Review.** Five review lenses read everything Smithy wrote. Smithy fixes the defects they find and tells you what changed.
5. **Hand-off.** Smithy validates the skill, offers a trigger eval, and tells you where the skill is and what to try first.

## In This Section

| Page | Read it when you want to |
| --- | --- |
| [Build Your First Skill](build-your-first-skill.md) | Go from an idea to a working skill, then a module |
| [Ways to Build a Skill](approaches.md) | Choose how a build runs |
| [Shapes of a Skill](shapes.md) | See what Smithy can make |
| [Work on an Existing Skill](modes.md) | Edit, convert, review, cut, package, or validate a skill |
| [Write a Good Skill](write-a-good-skill.md) | Learn the standard Smithy writes to and reviews against |
| [Subagent Patterns](subagent-patterns.md) | Spread a skill's work across subagents |
| [Make a Skill Customizable](make-a-skill-customizable.md) | Let teams change a skill without forking it |
| [Agents with Memory](agents-with-memory.md) | Build an agent that remembers you between sessions |
| [Modules and Registration](modules.md) | Decide how a skill registers with BMad |
| [Distribute Your Module](distribute-your-module.md) | Publish a module so others can install it |
| [Migrate an Old Module](migrate-an-old-module.md) | Bring a `module.yaml` module to the current format |
| [Eval Runner](bmad-eval.md) | Measure whether a skill works |

The exact file formats are in [Module Files](../reference/module-files.md) and [Eval Format](../reference/eval-format.md).
docs/toolsmith/write-a-good-skill.md:
---
title: 'Write a Good Skill'
description: 'The standard Smithy writes to and reviews against: outcomes over steps, what to cut, the description as the trigger, loading only what a run needs, and when to use a script.'
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

A skill is paid for on every run, in tokens and in the model's attention. A good skill holds what the model cannot work out for itself and little else. This page explains the standard Smithy writes to and reviews against, for when you write or judge a skill yourself.

## Write the Outcome, Not the Steps

Authors tend to script the path: phases, question banks, mandatory sections. A script is one imagined good session. Real sessions differ, and a model holding a script spends its effort on following it.

State where the work must end, and let the model find the way. An outcome-led skill holds five things:

| Part | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| Stance | Who the model is to the user |
| Outcome | What must exist at the end |
| Consumer | Who acts on it without having been in the conversation |
| Bar | What must be true of it for them |
| Non-inferables | Persona, conventions, wiring between systems, rules with consequences |

The consumer is the most useful line, because completeness, rigor, and tone all follow from it. A PRD that a team must act on without having heard the conversation has to state its scope and name its open questions. You do not need a step that says so.

## Cut What the Model Already Knows

Ask of every line whether a capable model would do this correctly without being told. If yes, cut it. A line stays only if you can name the different action the model takes without it.

Start each passage from one sentence that steers the model, then add a clause only when you can name the wrong action it prevents. A list of things the model could produce itself is explanation, not a rule.

Keep what the model cannot find by looking: the convention nobody wrote down, the reason behind a choice, the trap a config file does not reveal. Leave out what it can look up, such as a file's contents or a command's flags.

## Keep the Reason

Removing a reason is not leanness. A rule with its reason reaches cases you did not foresee, and a bare command gets applied literally. Replace all-caps MUST and NEVER with one sentence on the failure the rule prevents.

Say what to do instead of what to avoid, because a sentence about the wrong behavior puts it in front of the model. Keep a prohibition only when no positive form says the same thing.

## Make Instructions Easy to Follow

- **One topic to a paragraph.** A paragraph is a rule's scope, so a paragraph of several topics leaves the model guessing how far each rule reaches.
- **Number only true sequences.** Numbering tells the model that order matters. Use numbers for steps that feed each other, and bullets for independent ones.
- **End each step on something checkable.** "Once it is clear" lets the model declare itself done early. Name what must be true, in terms the model can verify.
- **Use one term for one thing.** Use a word the model already knows over a coined term, and keep using the same word.
- **Keep an example only if it fixes a shape.** A format line beats a worked sample. Try the rule alone first, and keep the smallest fragment that fixes what still goes wrong.

Give exact steps only where a wrong move costs something:

| Freedom | Use it when | Write |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High | Several approaches are valid | A goal in prose |
| Medium | A preferred pattern exists | A template or format |
| Low | The operation is fragile or must be consistent | An exact command or script |

## Make the Description the Trigger

The description is all the model sees when deciding whether to load a skill, and every installed description is paid for on every session. Write two parts: a five-to-eight-word summary in the third person, then `Use when the user says` with the quoted phrases people type.

```yaml
description: 'Writes customer release notes from merged pull requests. Use when the user says ''write the release notes'' or ''what shipped since the last tag''.'
```

- Give each phrase its own situation. Two wordings of one situation add length and no reach.
- Describe the user's problem, not a tool's symptom.
- Add `Not for ...`, naming the sibling skill, only when a skill is taking a neighbor's requests.
- Keep the procedure out. A description that explains the steps lets the model skip the body.
- For a skill only ever called by name, write one line and set `disable-model-invocation: true` where your tool supports it.

An agent is the exception on length. Its `Use when` starts with asking for it by name, then lists the phrases of every capability inside it. The validator enforces a ceiling of 1024 characters.

When a description fails, change its situations and boundaries. Do not paste the failed query into it. See [Eval Runner](bmad-eval.md#trigger-evals).

## Load Only What a Run Needs

`SKILL.md` is read on every run, and a reference is read only when its branch is reached. So the question is how much one run loads, not how big the skill is. A plain skill's entry aims near 800 tokens, and an agent's near 1,200. A complex workflow is the right size at any total when each branch sits in its own file.

- Split by relevance, not size. What only some branches need goes in a reference.
- Keep references one level deep. A reference never loads another.
- Name a reference when its branch is reached, not ahead of it.
- Make each file stand alone, because the entry can drop out of context.
- Hold every file a model reads to the same standard, including templates.

## Use Scripts for Work with One Right Answer

A script does work with one right answer per input: parsing, counting, resolving paths, validating structure, rendering a template. Prose does work that turns on meaning: judgment, tone, what to do with a result. Counting in prose costs tokens and comes out different each run. A script that decides what a sentence means breaks when the wording shifts.

A BMad script follows these rules:

- Python with a PEP 723 header, so `uv run` provides the dependencies and the user installs nothing.
- Run as `uv run {skill-root}/scripts/<name>.py`, never `python`, `pip`, or a bare `scripts/x.py`.
- `--help`, JSON on stdout when the agent reads the result, and a non-zero exit with a reason.
- Standard library first, with no network unless the docstring says why.
- A `unittest` test at `scripts/tests/test_<name>.py`, asserting what the script produced.
- No model ids, because users run any model.

## Patterns Worth Using

| Pattern | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Mine before you ask | Use what the user and the conversation already gave, then ask only for the gaps |
| Intent before reading | Learn why the user is here before scanning documents, so you can judge what matters |
| Capture without interrupting | Note information that arrives early, and use it when it becomes relevant |
| A gentle gate | Ask "anything else, or shall we move on?" at natural breaks instead of a hard menu |
| Plan, then change | Write the planned changes, validate them with a script, apply them, and verify the result |
| Two outputs | Pair a human document with a dense summary for downstream skills |
| Parallel review | Send several reviewers with different lenses before you finalize work |
| A sequential fallback | Run subagent work inline when subagents are unavailable, and say so |

## Test It Against the Smallest Version

You cannot judge a skill's structure from inside one run. Write a version of about five lines: role, outcome, consumer, and any rule whose absence has done damage. Run both on the same input.

| What you see | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| The small one wins | The structure was in the way, so cut it |
| They tie | The structure adds nothing you can see, so defend each line or remove it |
| The small one is rougher but recovers in a turn or two | You bought convenience, not quality, which is allowed |
| The small one stays materially worse | The structure earned its place, for now |

The bare model is the floor, and it rises with every release. When a skill stops beating it, retire the skill. A variant or baseline run in [`bmad-eval`](bmad-eval.md) does this comparison for you.
docs/start/build-your-first-change.md:
---
title: 'Getting Started'
description: Install BMad and build a small Python program
---

BMad can help you plan and build anything from a small bug fix to a project with
a million lines of code. Let's start with something small.

Already have a repository and a small change you want to make?
[Install BMad there](./install-bmad.md), open your coding tool in the
repository, and run the installed `bmad-build` skill. Talk to it about the
change you want, and it will make it happen.

Otherwise, start here. You will make a working Python program in an empty
project. This tutorial follows the
[one-session planning path](../plan/choose-a-planning-path.md): one
coherent request goes directly to the `bmad-build` skill.

:::note[Before You Start]
Use a macOS or Linux shell with Node.js 20.12+, Python 3, and a coding tool
supported by BMad. The exact install and launch commands below are for Claude
Code. If you use another supported tool, select it when installing BMad and run
the `bmad-build` skill there instead.
:::

## Create an Empty Project

```bash
mkdir bmad-first-project
cd bmad-first-project
```

:::caution[V7 Preview Alpha]
This tutorial uses v7 of BMad, which is in preview alpha and changes often. It suits solo or small teams that can pivot before beta; the v7 release ETA is mid-November 2026, and it might be sooner. If you need stability, run `npx bmad-method install` for the v6.12 release, frozen aside from bug fixes, and follow the [V6.12 documentation](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/tree/V6.12/docs/start).
:::

Install BMad Method with the skills CLI, then let the `bmad` skill set up the
project:

```bash
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/core-tools --skill '*'
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/method --skill '*'
```

Open your coding tool in this directory. For Claude Code, run:

```bash
claude
```

Then ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup`.

## Build a Mars Rover

Ask the `bmad-build` skill to make the
[Mars Rover programming kata](https://codingdojo.org/kata/mars-rover/), a small
exercise used to practice coding, without adding any design choices:

```text
/bmad-build write an implementation of mars rover kata
```

This gives the `bmad-build` skill room to ask what you want. It may start with a
question like this:

```text
`bmad-build`: Before implementation, I need one choice: which language should I use?
You: Python 3. Make it a small old-school terminal program I can run locally,
with no dependencies beyond Python standard library.
```

Your questions, answers, plan, and finished program may differ. Choose the
behavior you want rather than copying the example answer.

After you answer its questions, read its plan. Approve it or ask for changes.
The skill then writes the program, checks its work, fixes any problems, and
shows you what changed.

## Run the Mars Rover

Depending on what you told it, the result may look something like this:

```bash
python3 mars_rover.py --size 5x5 --obstacle 2,2
```

Enter `FFRFF`, then `MAP`, then `QUIT`. The terminal shows the rover stopping
before the obstacle:

```text
MARS ROVER CONTROL
Commands: F/M forward, B backward, L/R turn, MAP, STATUS, HELP, QUIT
Position: (0, 0)  Heading: N
rover> Position: (1, 2)  Heading: E
OBSTACLE: movement blocked at (2, 2)
rover>  4  . . . . .
 3  . . . . .
 2  . > # . .
 1  . . . . .
 0  . . . . .
    0 1 2 3 4
rover> Mission control signing off.
```

Open the files listed in the final message to look at your finished program.

## Ask BMad

The `bmad` skill answers questions about BMad. Use it to understand what
happened, decide what to do next, or solve a problem. Try it now:

```text
/bmad Explain what bmad-build just did.
```

## You Built It

Mars Rover showed how the `bmad-build` skill turns a short request into working
software. It clarified the request, presented a plan for your approval, wrote
the program, and checked its work before showing you the result.

## Keep Building

1. [Install BMad in your own repository](./install-bmad.md), then run
   the `bmad-build` skill with a short description of a small change.
   See [Build a Change](../build/build-a-change.md) for the attended path.
2. Continue to [Getting Deeper](../existing-codebases/getting-deeper.md) for a small change in a
   mature codebase, followed by a larger change using a written spec.
3. Use [Choose a Planning Path](../plan/choose-a-planning-path.md) when
   your next change may need several implementation sessions or multiple epics.
docs/start/get-answers-about-bmad.md:
---
title: 'Get Answers About BMad'
description: Use an LLM to quickly answer your own BMad questions
---

Use BMad's built-in help, source docs, or the community to get answers — from quickest to most thorough.

## 1. Ask BMad

The fastest way to get answers. The `bmad` skill is available directly in your AI session and handles over 80% of questions — it reads your active initiative, sees which `<type>-<slug>/` documents are already written, and tells you what to do next.

```
bmad I have a SaaS idea and know all the features. Where do I start?
bmad What are my options for UX design?
bmad I'm stuck on the PRD workflow
```

:::tip
You can also use `/bmad` or `$bmad` depending on your platform, but just `bmad` should work everywhere. The same skill runs `bmad setup`, `bmad status`, and `bmad migrate method`, and switches the active initiative.
:::

## 2. Go Deeper with Source

The `bmad` skill draws on your installed configuration. For questions about BMad's internals, history, or architecture — or if you're researching BMad before installing — point your AI at the source directly.

Clone or open the [BMAD-METHOD repo](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD) and ask your AI about it. Any agent-capable tool (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.) can read the source and answer questions directly.

:::note[Example]
**Q:** "Tell me the fastest way to build something with BMad"

**A:** Run `bmad-build`. Give it direct intent, an issue, a spec, or a planned story; it uses the available context and chooses the clarification, planning, implementation, and review depth needed.
:::

**Tips for better answers:**

- **Be specific** — "What does step 3 of the PRD workflow do?" beats "How does PRD work?"
- **Verify surprising claims** — LLMs occasionally get things wrong. Check the source file or ask on Discord.

### Not using an agent? Use the docs site

If your AI can't read local files (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, etc.), open [the BMad docs site](https://docs.bmad-method.org/).

## 3. Ask Someone

If neither the `bmad` skill nor the source answered your question, you now have a much better question to ask.

| Channel                 | Use For                    |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `help-requests` forum   | Questions                  |
| `#suggestions-feedback` | Ideas and feature requests |

**Discord:** [discord.gg/gk8jAdXWmj](https://discord.gg/gk8jAdXWmj)

**GitHub Issues:** [github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/issues](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/issues)

_You!_  
  _Stuck_  
    _in the queue—_  
      _waiting_  
        _for who?_

_The source_  
  _is there,_  
    _plain to see!_

_Point_  
  _your machine._  
    _Set it free._

_It reads._  
  _It speaks._  
    _Ask away—_

_Why wait_  
  _for tomorrow_  
    _when you have_  
      _today?_

        _—Claude_
docs/start/install-bmad.md:
---
title: 'How to Install BMad'
description: Install the stable BMad release or the preview skills, set up the project runtime, and verify or update it.
---

Install BMad through the Skills CLI, then run `bmad setup` in the project.

:::caution[V7 Preview Alpha]
This page installs v7 of BMad, which is in preview alpha. Its skills, install path, and documentation change often, and updates can break an existing setup. It is recommended for solo or small teams that can pivot as things will change before beta. The v7 release ETA is mid-November 2026, and it might be sooner. If you need stability until v7 is finalized for release, install v6.12 instead.
:::

## Install the Stable Release

The stable release is v6.12, frozen aside from bug fixes. With [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 20.12+, [Python](https://www.python.org) 3.10+, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), run in your project:

```bash
npx bmad-method install
```

The rest of this page does not apply to v6.12. Its source and documentation live on the [V6.12 branch](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/tree/V6.12).

## Prerequisites

You need an AI coding tool that supports skills and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) for setup and Python scripts. The Skills CLI also needs Node.js, npm, and Git.

## Install the Skills

From your project directory, run:

```bash
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/core-tools --skill '*'
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/method --skill '*'
```

Each module sits in its own folder of the repository, and each command installs one module whole, its record included. `--skill '*'` takes every skill in the folder; the Skills CLI still asks which coding tools to install to. Core tools hold the `bmad` skill for setup and help, so every install needs them. Add Toolsmith (`skills/toolsmith`) or Founder (`skills/founder`) the same way.

To choose skills instead, run `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD` and select your coding tool and skills. Include `bmad` for setup and help, and the module records `bmod-core-tools` and `bmod-method` for the modules you use. To install a small set by name:

```bash
npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD --skill bmad --skill bmod-core-tools --skill bmod-method --skill bmad-build --skill bmad-agent-po
```

Add review, retrospective, or other skills as needed. Keep project and global installation scopes consistent.

## Security Scan Warnings

During install, the Skills CLI shows a Security Risk Assessments table from three scanners: Gen Agent Trust Hub, Socket, and Snyk. Some BMad skills get a Med Risk or High Risk rating. The scanners flag behavior the skills use on purpose:

- Skills run Python scripts from the project's `_bmad/scripts/` folder with `uv run` to load configuration and customizations.
- Customization files under `_bmad/custom/` can add activation steps that the skill runs.
- Some skills read text written by other people, such as tickets, issues, and pull request diffs, which scanners treat as a prompt injection risk.
- Some skills tell you to install a missing skill with `npx skills add`.

Skills run with your coding tool's permissions, so add only customizations you trust. The full report for each skill is on [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD).

## Set Up and Verify

Open the coding tool from the project folder and ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup`. Setup installs the shared runtime and module scripts under `_bmad/`. Ask for `bmad status` to verify the installation and versions. Documents and tickets go to `_bmad-output`, inside the active initiative's folder when one is set; ask `bmad` to create or switch one.

Invoke `bmad-build` with the change you want, or ask `bmad` for guidance. For work spanning repositories, set up at the workspace root so skills can reach both the output folder and code repositories.

## Update an Installation

Ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup` again. It checks each module's version and runs `npx skills update` for you when there is a newer one. Then it asks any new config questions, moves your `_bmad/custom/` files when a skill was renamed, and offers to delete skills a module renamed or removed. Last, it checks whether a migration applies and asks whether to run it.

If you update by hand with `npx skills update`, run `bmad setup` afterwards. Restart your coding tool when its skill catalog needs refreshing.

## What You Get

Your coding tool discovers the installed skills. The project's `_bmad/` holds shared configuration and supporting scripts. Team and personal customizations live under `_bmad/custom/` and survive setup refreshes.
docs/reference/document-templates.md:
---
title: Document Templates
description: The templates that ship with bmad-facilitate, and which one shows each thing a template can do.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

Use this page to find a shipped template to copy, or to see how a template does something you want. Modules ship them, each in the `doc-templates/` folder beside its `bmod.toml` in your skills folder: `bmod-method`, `bmad-founder-agent-advisor` or `bmod-cis`.

To change one for your team, extend it instead of copying it, so its updates keep arriving; [Customize a Document for Your Team](../customize/customize-a-document-for-your-team.md) shows how. To start a different document from one, copy it into `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/` with a new `template:` id and edit the copy. [Write a Document Template](../customize/write-a-document-template.md) covers the file format.

## Shipped templates

| Template | Module | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decision-record` | BMad Method | Recording a choice, the alternatives and what it costs |
| `postmortem` | BMad Method | Learning from something that went wrong, without blame |
