| `security-review` | BMad Method | Checking a system against the OWASP Top 10 or STRIDE |
| `proposal` | Founder | Asking for money, time or approval |
| `pitch-deck` | Founder | A talk or pitch with slides |
| `accelerator-application` | Founder | An application to an accelerator, in the program's own questions |
| `board-pack` | Founder | The pre-read sent before a board meeting |
| `cofounder-agreement` | Founder | Co-founders agreeing roles, decisions, equity and leaving before a lawyer drafts |
| `customer-interview-script` | Founder | A customer interview guide built on past behaviour |
| `first-hire` | Founder | Deciding whether to hire now, and the scorecard, cost and test for the role |
| `fundraising-plan` | Founder | Planning a raise: amount, milestones, instrument, investors and stop date |
| `ideal-customer` | Founder | The first narrow group of customers to win and how to reach them |
| `investor-update` | Founder | The monthly or quarterly update to investors and advisors |
| `launch-plan` | Founder | Taking a product to market |
| `lean-canvas` | Founder | The whole business model on one page, with its riskiest assumption |
| `ninety-day-plan` | Founder | Two or three goals for the next ninety days, with metrics and owners |
| `positioning` | Founder | Positioning and the one-liner |
| `pricing` | Founder | How the product is priced and how the price is tested |
| `startup-diagnostic` | Founder | Hard questions on whether an idea has real demand, ending in one dated assignment |
| `validation-experiment` | Founder | Testing whether people will pay or act, with the pass mark set first |
| `character` | Creative Intelligence Suite 0.4.0 and later | A fictional character for a story, game or campaign, on a one-page sheet |

The BMad Method also ships the planning templates John (`bmad-agent-pm`) and Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`) run, `brief`, `prfaq` and `brd` among them; see [Define Requirements and a Specification](../plan/define-requirements-and-a-specification.md).

## What a template can do

| To do this | Look at | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Press the user on a thin answer | `postmortem`, Contributing factors | The section comment says when to push and what to ask |
| Make the user pick from a list | `decision-record`, Status | The section comment names the allowed values |
| Make the user pick from a source | `security-review`, Scope and system | The section comment points at the method catalog |
| Drive questions from a catalog | `security-review`, `methods-security.csv` | The `methods` frontmatter names a CSV of key questions |
| Walk the sections in order, each with its own voice | `prfaq` in `bmad-agent-analyst/assets/` | `paced: true` in the frontmatter, and each section comment is the brief for that part |
| Change how a path runs | `security-review`, `stance` | The comment says what the fast path does for this document |
| Use the shared planning rules | Any shipped template | `guidance: guidance-planning` adds stakes levels, `[ASSUMPTION]` tags in the body, ids and testable requirements |
| Review against its own rubric | `proposal`, `rubric-proposal.md` | The `rubric` frontmatter names the file |
| Set the order and what is required | Any shipped template | `facilitation_order` lists the sections by id, `?` on those not required |
| Include a section only when it applies | `proposal`, Alternatives | `alternatives?` in the order and an `include when:` section comment |
| Draw a diagram | `postmortem`, Timeline | A `diagram:` kind in the section comment |
| Add a table of contents | `proposal` | A bare `## Table of Contents` heading after the title |
| Render as slides | `pitch-deck` | `view: slides` in the frontmatter |
| Always make the view | `pitch-deck` | `html_view: always` in the frontmatter, because the slides are the deliverable |
| Render the same layout every time | `prfaq` in `bmad-agent-analyst/assets/`, `prfaq-view.html`; also `brief` and John's `pitch` | `view` names an HTML file whose slots a script fills at close |
| Have a page written for each document | `character`, `character-sheet.html` | `view` names a starter, and a `view` comment gives the brief |
| Have a page written from a brief alone | Founder's templates, such as `pitch-deck` | A `view` comment with no `view` file says where to be creative |
| Propose rather than only ask | `character`, `stance` | The comment invites proposals; one the user accepts is theirs |
| Write several files | `postmortem`, `companions` | The comment says when to write the customer notice and what it holds |

No shipped template adds to another. [Extend a template](../customize/write-a-document-template.md#extend-a-template) shows how.
docs/reference/eval-format.md:
---
title: Eval Format
description: 'The files bmad-eval reads and writes: cases, trigger queries, rubric expectations, runner commands, harness keys, and run folders.'
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

Use this page for the exact formats `bmad-eval` reads and writes. For when to run which mode, see [Eval Runner](../toolsmith/bmad-eval.md).

## File Layout

```text
<skill>/
└── evals/
    ├── cases.json        # baseline, variant, and quality cases
    └── triggers.json     # trigger queries
```

`bmad-eval` looks for cases in the file you name, then `<skill>/evals/`, then `<project-root>/evals/<skill-name>/`, then anywhere under `<project-root>/evals/`.

## Cases

`cases.json` is a JSON array of cases, or an object with a `cases` array. One case looks like this:

```json
{
  "id": "create-1",
  "input": "I want a brief for InsuLens, a claims-triage tool for mid-market insurers. Notes are in evals/insulens/files/memo.md",
  "rubric": [
    "brief.md exists and its word count is between 250 and 1500",
    "brief.md names InsuLens and the mid-market insurer segment"
  ],
  "state_prefix": null,
  "files": ["evals/insulens/files/memo.md"]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable identifier, used as the case's folder name in the run |
| `input` | The realistic user request, sent as given after any `state_prefix` |
| `rubric` | Named expectations, each graded to `{text, passed, evidence}` |
| `state_prefix` | Optional bracketed text that places the skill mid-workflow. Null or absent starts cold |
| `files` | Optional fixtures staged into the clean working directory |

Each entry in `files` is a path relative to `--project-root` or the cases file's folder, or a GitHub file URL pinned to a commit or tag, `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<ref>/<path>`, for data kept in another repo. A relative path keeps its folders, so the input can name it as written; a GitHub file lands at the workspace root under its file name. Absolute and `~` paths are refused so the cases run on anyone's machine, and a missing fixture stops the run before any case starts.

## `state_prefix`

The runner prepends the prefix to `input` and sends the result as one message, so one case can test any mid-workflow moment.

```text
[the skill has already worked through discovery; on turn 4 the user was asked about stakeholders and responded:] User said: "just me and a PM"
```

Only a case where the conversation itself is the deliverable needs real multiple turns.

## Trigger Queries

`triggers.json` is a JSON array of `{query, should_trigger}` records.

```json
[
  { "query": "help me turn my deploy script into a reusable skill", "should_trigger": true },
  { "query": "my deploy script keeps failing on the rollback step", "should_trigger": false }
]
```

Aim for about twenty queries, roughly half of each kind, varied in form. Make the should-not queries near misses that share keywords and domain with the real ones.

## Strong and Weak Expectations

A wrong output must not be able to pass an expectation. A weak one is worse than none, because a passing check reads as proof.

| Weak | Why |
| --- | --- |
| "brief.md exists" | Passes for an empty file. Pair it with a content check |
| "the brief is high quality" | Cannot be graded. State the property concretely |
| Anything that follows from understanding the prompt | Proves nothing |

| Strong | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Specific facts | "incorporates at least two findings from section X" |
| Structure | "word count between 250 and 1500" |
| Negative assertions | "does not introduce content from unrelated sections" |
| Frontmatter | "frontmatter contains title, status, created, updated" |
| Bounded output | "the final message contains a JSON object with intent='create'" |
| Side artifacts | ".memlog.md captures the pricing decision with its rejected alternative" |
| Tool calls | "the transcript contains a call invoking bmad-editorial-review-prose" |
| Phase order | "the polish call occurs after the brief Write and before the final JSON block" |
| Read-only inputs | "the input is byte-identical to the fixture" |

## Non-Interactive Runs

Single-shot modes need the skill to finish without stopping to ask. Start the input with the literal `Run headless.`, use a keyword from the skill's own headless section, or give enough context that no question is needed. A `state_prefix` can also supply the answer the skill would ask for. A skill with no headless path needs a headless mode, or a human in the loop for that case.

## Runner Commands

Agents run these for you. They are listed for reading a run or running one by hand.

Baseline, variant, and quality:

```bash
uv run {skill-root}/scripts/run_evals.py \
  --cases <cases-file> --skill-path <skill> --output-dir <dir> \
  --mode quality|baseline|variant [--variant-path <skill>] \
  --label <skill-name>-<mode> [--runs N]
```

Trigger:

```bash
uv run {skill-root}/scripts/run_triggers.py \
  --skill-path <skill> --queries <queries-file> --output-dir <dir> \
  [--runs-per-query N]
```

Aggregate the time, tokens, and tool calls of repeated runs into mean, sample standard deviation, min, max, and delta:

```bash
uv run {skill-root}/scripts/aggregate_benchmark.py --baseline <run-dir>/<config-a> --variant <run-dir>/<config-b>
```

Convert a skill-creator file, or add `--to skill-creator` to reverse it:

```bash
uv run {skill-root}/scripts/convert_cases.py <evals.json> --output <cases.json>
```

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | The run completed. A trigger query failing its threshold is a result, not an error |
| 1 | A case errored or timed out, or the command was not found |
| 2 | Usage error |
| 3 | No harness is recorded |

`--runs` defaults to 1, which counts as a quick look. A result is settled at 3 or more.

## Harness Keys

The harness is the coding tool that evals run through. These keys are recorded under `[workflow.harness]` in `bmad-eval`'s customization. In a project without BMad, write the same keys to a JSON file and pass its path with `--harness`.

| Key | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `command` | The argv for one non-interactive run, with `{prompt}` standing for the input and the flag that turns off permission prompts |
| `skill_dir` | The folder under the workspace that the tool reads skills from |
| `env` | Environment variables a run needs. A value is set as given, `~` means the fresh home folder, and an empty value forwards the host's |
| `home_files` | Files or folders under your home that keep you logged in, placed at the same path in the fresh home folder |

```toml
[workflow.harness]
command = ["claude", "-p", "{prompt}", "--output-format", "stream-json", "--verbose", "--dangerously-skip-permissions"]
skill_dir = ".claude/skills"
env = { USER = "" }
home_files = ["Library/Keychains"]
```

## Run Folders

Each run is a dated folder under the output folder, which is the configured reports folder when BMad is set up and `~/bmad-evals/` otherwise. `run.json` names the harness command. Each case folder, and each trigger attempt, holds:

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| The prompt | What was sent |
| The transcript | What the harness printed |
| `stderr.txt` | The error stream |
| `cwd/` | The workspace after the run |
| `timing.json` | Timing, written when the invocation ends |
| `grading.json` | Grades, when quality mode ran |

Run folders are never deleted, overwritten, or rotated.
docs/reference/module-files.md:
---
title: Module Files
description: 'The files that make a BMad module: bmod.toml, roster.toml, retired.toml, migration files, and help, with every key and rule.'
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

Use this page for the exact keys in a module's files. For what a module is and how to choose a registration, see [Modules and Registration](../toolsmith/modules.md). Smithy writes these files for you, and `validate_manifests.py` checks them.

## Where the Files Live

| File | Multi-skill module | Single-skill module |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bmod.toml` with `[bmod]` | In the `bmod-<code>` record folder | In the skill's folder |
| `bmod.toml` with `[skill]` | In each member's folder | The same file, with `[skill]` empty |
| `help/help.md` | In the record folder | In the skill's folder |
| `SKILL.md` | The record has one that only redirects to `bmad setup <code>` | The skill's own |
| `roster.toml`, `retired.toml`, `migration-<n>.toml` | In the record folder | Beside `bmod.toml` |

`bmad` finds a module by its `[bmod]` table. Validation requires a multi-skill record folder to be named `bmod-<code>`, and a single-skill module's folder keeps the skill's name.

## `bmod.toml`

A file holds a `[bmod]` table, a `[skill]` table, or both.

### `[bmod]`

| Key | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | Yes | Configuration namespace and the name in `bmad setup <code>`. Cannot be `_config`, `custom`, `modules`, or `scripts` |
| `version` | Yes | The module's version, compared with its source to offer updates |
| `update_source` | Yes | Where updates come from. Starts with `github:`, `https://`, `file:`, or `plugin:` |
| `skills` | Multi-skill | Every member skill |
| `required_skills` | No | Skills the module needs, see [Dependencies](#dependencies) |
| `recommended_skills` | No | Skills that help beside it. Setup reports them and does not insist |
| `pre_install_message` | For validation | Shown before an update, or before `bmad` installs the record itself |
| `post_install_message` | For validation | Shown after installing |

Setup accepts a record without the install messages, but `validate_manifests.py` requires both keys, empty if unused.

A `github:` source is `github:<owner>/<repo>/<path>`, where `<path>` is the folder holding the skill folders, such as `skills`. With no path, the repository root is the skill. Update checks read `bmod.toml` from the `main` branch.

### `[[bmod.config_questions]]`

Each entry is one question for `bmad setup <code>`, asked in file order.

| Key | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | Yes | Dotted key, read as `modules.<code>.<key>`. Must not be the code or start with `<code>.` |
| `prompt` | Yes | The question text |
| `default` | Yes | The default answer, with `{project-root}` kept literal |
| `scope` | No | `team`, the default, or `user` for a personal answer that is not committed |

No other keys are allowed.

### `[[bmod.knowledge]]`

Optional. Lists extra help documents inside the record folder, with `path` and `skills`. `skills` is `"*"`, the default, or a list of skill names.

### `[skill]`

| Key | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bmod` | In a member file | The record folder, such as `bmod-acme` |
| `source` | In a member file | Must equal the record's `update_source` |
| `required_skills` | No | What this skill alone requires |
| `recommended_skills` | No | What helps beside this skill |
| `scripts` | No | Paths written like `scripts/foo.py` that setup installs to `_bmad/<code>/scripts/` |

In a single-skill module, leave `[skill]` empty unless it declares `scripts`, because the record in the same file already names the module's one skill.

### Dependencies

A plain name is a skill from the same source. A table names a skill from elsewhere.

```toml
required_skills = [
  "acme-release-notes",
  { skill = "bmad", version = "6.13.0", source = "github:bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/core-tools" },
]
```

`version` is optional. Module-wide needs go in `[bmod]`, including all of a single-skill module's needs. One member's needs go in its `[skill]` table.

### Examples

A record:

```toml
[bmod]
code = "acme"
version = "1.0.0"
update_source = "github:acme/skills/skills"
skills = ["acme-release-notes", "acme-agent-scout"]
required_skills = [{ skill = "bmad", version = "6.13.0", source = "github:bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/core-tools" }]
pre_install_message = ""
post_install_message = ""

[[bmod.config_questions]]
key = "release_folder"
prompt = "Where should release notes go?"
default = "{project-root}/docs/releases"
```

A member:

```toml
[skill]
bmod = "bmod-acme"
source = "github:acme/skills/skills"
```

A single-skill module:

```toml
[bmod]
code = "acme"
version = "0.1.0"
update_source = "github:acme/acme-release-notes/skills"
required_skills = [{ skill = "bmad", version = "6.13.0", source = "github:bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/core-tools" }]
pre_install_message = ""
post_install_message = ""

[skill]
```

## Reading Answers

A skill reads a setup answer with one call, listing every key it needs.

```bash
uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_config.py --project-root {project-root} --key modules.acme.release_folder
```

## `roster.toml`

Required when a member is an agent. It is how `bmad` and party mode know who is available. A member with `skill` is an agent, present only while that skill is installed. A member without `skill` is a guest who exists only in groups.

```toml
[[members]]
code = "acme-agent-scout"
skill = "acme-agent-scout"
name = "Scout"
icon = "🔭"
title = "Release Scout"
persona = "Two sentences on who this agent is."

[[groups]]
id = "release-team"
name = "Release Team"
scene = "A release readiness meeting."
members = ["acme-agent-scout"]
memory = false
```

## `retired.toml`

Lists skills the module no longer ships. `bmad setup` offers to delete any still installed, and moves a renamed skill's `_bmad/custom/` files to the new name. A retired name is never reused, and a name can appear only once.

```toml
renamed = [{ from = "acme-notes", to = "acme-release-notes" }]
removed = ["acme-old-check"]
```

## `migration-<n>.toml`

A module ships a migration beside its `bmod.toml`, and `bmad migrate` runs them in `<n>` order. The file has a `[migration]` table with `module`, `from`, `to`, `title`, `summary`, `detect`, `guide`, and a `checklist` array. A file missing any of these is not listed. The file holds the rules, and `bmad` follows them.

## Help Files

`help/help.md` covers the whole module and is read by the `bmad` skill. Every other `help/*.md` is a topic file, read only when `help.md` names it. See [Write the Help](../toolsmith/modules.md#write-the-help).

## Validate

In a repository with `skills/*/bmod.toml`:

```bash
uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/validate_manifests.py --project-root <repo>
```

It covers manifests, membership, versions, retired names, help topics, and the roster.
docs/reference/skills-and-agents.md:
---
title: Skills and Agents
description: What a BMad skill is, how to invoke one, where the installer puts them, which agents exist with their menu codes, and what each core skill does.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

Use this page to find out what skills and agents a BMad install gives you and how to start each one. How a skill is used in practice lives on its chapter page, linked from the tables below.

## What a Skill Is

A skill is a named command the installer places in your AI tool. Type its name — `bmad`, for example — and the tool loads it. On some platforms the name takes a `/` or `$` prefix.

A skill does one of three things: loads an agent persona, runs a multi-step workflow, or runs a single task.

## Skills vs. Agent Menu Triggers

BMad offers two ways to start work.

| Mechanism              | How you invoke it                                     | What happens                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Skill**              | Type the skill name (e.g. `bmad`) in your AI tool     | Directly loads an agent, runs a workflow, or runs a task          |
| **Agent menu trigger** | Load an agent first, then type a code (e.g. `CREATE`) | The agent starts the matching workflow while staying in character |

Use a skill when you know which workflow you want. Use a trigger when you are already working with an agent and want to switch tasks without leaving the conversation.

## Where Skills Live

The installer writes one directory per skill, each holding a `SKILL.md`, into a directory that depends on your tool:

| Tool                                                  | Skills directory  |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Claude Code                                           | `.claude/skills/` |
| Cursor, Windsurf, Codex, Auggie, Amp, and most others | `.agents/skills/` |
| Cline                                                 | `.cline/skills/`  |
| IBM Bob                                               | `.bob/skills/`    |
| Antigravity                                           | `.agent/skills/`  |
| AdaL                                                  | `.adal/skills/`   |

Some other tools also use their own directory, and a global install goes to a per-user directory instead. The installer output names the exact path for the tool you chose. The directory name is the skill name: `bmad-agent-dev/` registers `bmad-agent-dev`.

:::tip[The installed directories are the canonical list]
Open your skills directory to see every installed skill with its description. Run `bmad` for guidance on which to use next.
:::

## Agents

The BMad Method module installs six named agents. Load one with its skill ID, then say what you want or type a code from its menu. Agents show the menu only when you ask what they can do. Codes are scoped to the agent that shows them: `VALIDATE` reviews a document for John and Mary and checks the ticket tree for Sofia. Asked what they can do, John and Mary also list the documents they write, including any your team added.

| Agent                  | Skill ID                 | Codes                                                               | Menu                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Analyst (Mary)         | `bmad-agent-analyst`     | `BRAINSTORM`, `RESEARCH`, `CREATE`, `UPDATE`, `VALIDATE`, `CONTEXT` | Brainstorm; research a market, domain, technology, competitors or users, or choose between options; create, update or validate a brief, PRFAQ, BRD or a document your team added; project context |
| Product Manager (John) | `bmad-agent-pm`          | `CREATE`, `UPDATE`, `VALIDATE`                                      | Create or update a PRD or one of eleven more planning documents; validate one into review findings                                                                                           |
| Product Owner (Sofia)  | `bmad-agent-po`          | `SPEC`, `TICKETS`, `REFINE`, `BOARD`, `VALIDATE`, `REPLAN`, `STORE` | Requirements from a PRD, brief, or notes into a ticket; slice an initiative or epic; refine a ticket; the board; validation; replan a mid-flight change; tracker setup                            |
| Architect (Winston)    | `bmad-agent-architect`   | `ARCHITECTURE`                                                      | Architecture spine                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Developer (Amelia)     | `bmad-agent-dev`         | `BUILD`, `TESTS`, `REVIEW`, `RETRO`                                 | Build; QA test generation; code review; epic retrospective                                                                                                                                        |
| UX Designer (Sally)    | `bmad-agent-ux-designer` | `DESIGN`                                                            | UX design                                                                                                                                                                                         |

The Founder module adds Nadia the Founder Advisor (`bmad-founder-agent-advisor`). An experienced founder who coaches others, she tests whether an idea has demand, coaches seventeen business documents through `bmad-facilitate` (from a startup diagnostic and pricing to a fundraising plan, pitch deck and board pack), runs runway, unit economics and cap table math by script, turns customer interviews into evidence, works the investor pipeline with meeting prep and an objection bank, reads term sheets in plain words, and hosts a pitch room where investor personas make offers or pass. She keeps the company's facts, the funders and the decisions in a business record folder you choose at `bmad setup founder` (default `company/`), so every document quotes the same figures and any agent can read them. Install Founder in the folder where you plan the business, such as a notes vault, and ask for Nadia, the founder advisor or the advisor.

:::note[Where is Paige?]
The Technical Writer (Paige) is on hiatus. Project context lives on: use the Analyst's `CONTEXT` code or invoke `bmad-project-context` directly.
:::

The Developer's `TESTS` code runs `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests`; the full Test Architect is a separate module. See [Test Completed Work](../build/test-completed-work.md).

Each agent is an identity plus a customizable layer. See [Customize BMad](../customize/customize-bmad.md) for how that model works and how to change an agent.

## Core Skills

Every installation includes the core module: eleven skills that work in any project, any module, any phase. No agent session is required.

### bmad

The BMad hub. Ask it a question and it answers from the installed modules and recommends the next skill: it reads the active initiative, lists the `<type>-<slug>/` folders already written there, and puts the next steps in priority order with their skill commands. It also runs `bmad setup` and `bmad status` for the project's runtime, `bmad migrate method` to move a v6 project onto the current layout, and shows, switches, creates, or clears the active initiative.

**Input:** a question in plain language, or one of the commands above. **Output:** an answer with the prioritized next steps, or the command's result.

:::note[Example]
`bmad I have a SaaS idea and know all the features. Where do I start?`
:::

### bmad-advanced-elicitation

A push on a draft you have in front of you. A first draft is the model's most likely answer; this skill moves it off center in chosen directions, through independent readers who hold none of the author's reasons, and proposes a revision you accept or reject. The draft can be the model's or yours: a section, a plan, a decision, a pasted document.

**Use it when:**

- Output seems fine but you suspect there is more
- You want assumptions stressed, the premise questioned, or the other side argued
- The work matters enough to spend a few minutes pushing it

**Skip it when:**

- It is one quick choice you want reconsidered: asking the model to push harder and consider alternatives is often as good, and much faster

**How it works:**

1. It names the target and where it is probably weak, and starts three pushes right away, each from a different direction (what is wrong, what is missing, the premise, simplicity, the future, the other side): the method that best fits the weak spot, a wildcard chosen to take the work somewhere unexpected, and, for a single choice, an open push to reconsider it with everything the conversation holds, or for a document, a second method
2. Methods you name when you call it run instead, and a team or person can set default methods with `bmad-customize`. Ask it to list the methods to see what else is there
3. Each method runs as its own independent reader, all at once, in the method's own form: a pre-mortem is written from after the failure, a stakeholder speaks in their own voice
4. You get one proposed revision as a numbered list of changes, each tagged with the push that drove it, with the full revised passages and every push's findings in a report beside it. Accept all, some by number, reject, or rerun a push with direction, then take another round or finish

Methods include pre-mortem, first principles, inversion, red team, steelman, Socratic questioning, assumption audit, stakeholder lens, subtraction, and more; teams add their own.

The brief, PRD, UX and architecture skills and the agent personas remind you it is there; you can also start it yourself by saying "advanced elicitation". With nothing named, it pushes what you were just discussing, at its own size: a choice is pushed as a choice, not as the plan around it. Name a target ("advanced elicitation on section 4") or methods ("with pre-mortem and red team") to aim it.

### bmad-review

Reviews a diff, document, or other artifact through one or more lenses and reports every finding in one shape. Zero findings is a valid outcome; it never pads to look thorough.

| Lens                 | Applies to | Method                                                                                 |
| -------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Adversarial**      | Anything   | Forced-finding review that looks for what is missing, not only what is wrong           |
| **Edge case**        | Anything   | Walks every branching path and boundary condition in content that defines behavior     |
| **Verification gap** | Code       | Finds changed behavior that could regress without reliable verification catching it    |
| **Structure**        | Documents  | Proposes cuts, merges, moves, and condensing                                           |
| **Prose**            | Documents  | Copy-edits for issues that impede comprehension; runs on top of the structure findings |

The two editorial lenses hold content sacrosanct: they critique only how a document is organized and expressed, and they propose changes rather than making them. The lens set is not fixed; a `customize.toml` override can add lenses or replace shipped ones.

**Input:** the content (a diff, branch, uncommitted changes, file, or document) and optionally the lenses to run. **Output:** findings grouped by lens, as JSON, markdown, or both.

:::note[Who runs it]
`bmad-retrospective` runs the code lenses over a completed epic's diff. `bmad-facilitate`, which runs John's and Mary's documents, and the UX and architecture skills run the editorial lenses at their finalize step. `bmad-build` and `bmad-code-review` use their own reviewer layers; see [Review a Change](../build/review-a-change.md).
:::

### bmad-customize

Writes and verifies customization overrides for installed skills, so you can change an agent's or workflow's behavior without hand-authoring TOML. Describe the change in plain language; it selects the right scope, writes the override under `_bmad/custom/`, and verifies the merged result. See [Customize BMad](../customize/customize-bmad.md).

### bmad-brainstorming

Facilitates a brainstorming session using proven creative techniques, guiding you toward 100 or more ideas before organizing them. It shifts creative domain periodically to prevent clustering.

**Input:** a topic or problem statement, plus optional context. **Output:** a self-contained `brainstorm.html` keepsake and an optional `brainstorm-<topic>.md` for downstream skills. See [Explore and Validate an Idea](../plan/explore-and-validate-an-idea.md).

### bmad-deep-recon

Researches a topic to support a decision, three ways: drafts a research prompt for the tool you already use, turns a finished report into a cited summary other skills consume, or runs the research here with parallel web searches. Built-in types cover market, domain, technical, competitive, user-voice, and academic literature research, plus choosing between candidates. It also answers questions about your own repository from its code and git history: a question one file answers gets a cited answer in chat, and anything larger a document that cites a line or commit for every claim and that `bmad-build` reads as evidence.

**Output:** a cited `research-<topic>.md` and an optional HTML briefing; codebase research also writes each decision record you approve. See [Research a Decision](../plan/research-a-decision.md).

### bmad-forge-idea

Pressure-tests a half-formed idea in a questioning conversation, one question at a time, with different personas probing its weak points, until you can act on it or drop it with confidence.

**Output:** a `forge-report.html` keepsake every run, plus a `forge-<slug>.md` brief when the idea hardens. See [Explore and Validate an Idea](../plan/explore-and-validate-an-idea.md#pressure-test-an-idea-with-forge-idea).

### bmad-facilitate

Coaches you through one document from a template library, then updates or validates it. It reads your inputs, asks only what you alone know, reviews the draft against a rubric, and polishes it. Rigor follows the stakes you state. It ships no templates itself; modules do. The BMad Method adds `decision-record`, `postmortem` and `security-review`, the Founder module adds seventeen business templates such as `startup-diagnostic`, `pricing`, `fundraising-plan`, `proposal` and `pitch-deck`, and the Creative Intelligence Suite adds `character` from its 0.4.0 release. Your team can add its own, replace a shipped one, or add rules to one; see [Write a Document Template](../customize/write-a-document-template.md). Planning documents such as PRDs belong to John (`bmad-agent-pm`), the brief, the PRFAQ and the BRD to Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`), and the Founder templates to Nadia (`bmad-founder-agent-advisor`).

**Output:** `<id>-<slug>.md` with a `.memlog.md` and review files in its own folder, any companion files the template asks for, and an optional HTML view, which a pitch deck renders as slides.

:::note[Example]
`bmad-facilitate coach me through a security review covering the OWASP Top 10, output to docs/owasp`
:::

### bmad-party-mode

Puts your installed agents, or custom personas, in one conversation, in character, with you steering. A mode setting decides whether one model voices everyone or separate agents think independently, and you can save custom parties for reuse. See [Run Multi-Agent Discussions](../customize/run-multi-agent-discussions.md).

### bmad-shard-pro

Makes a long document, such as a large PRD, architecture or manual, cheap for an agent to navigate. It assesses the document first and recommends one of three outcomes: leave it as it is, add a detailed contents list with line ranges, or split it word for word into a map and shards. It never rewrites content: a script does the cutting and checks that nothing was lost. Each shard's frontmatter links back to the main file and holds its map entry, so any agent can change the document by following the note in the main file; running the skill again rebuilds the map from the shards and rechecks them. A long document that is kept and edited is split, and one that has to stay one file gets a contents list; see [Prepare Long Documents for Agents](../plan/prepare-long-documents-for-agents.md). Transcripts, chat exports and meeting notes go to `bmad-ingest` instead.

**Input:** a markdown or text document; convert other formats first. **Output:** in the document's own folder, a main file named after the folder holding a note and the map, the shards, the frozen original in `.source/`, and an entry in its `.memlog.md`; or, for a contents list, the same file with the list added.

### bmad-ingest

Turns raw input, such as a meeting transcript, a chat or email thread, a voice memo or a long document, into a note that an agent or person reads instead of the raw. It picks a note template by the template's description.

- Core tools ship `meeting`, `thread`, `voice-memo`, `document` and `one-on-one`.
- The BMad Method adds `standup`, `retrospective`, `sprint-review`, `discovery-workshop` and `user-interview`.
- You add your own in the project's `_bmad/custom/ingest-templates/`, in `~/.bmad/ingest-templates/` for every project, from a GitHub URL, or in any module's `ingest-templates/` folder. A project's template wins over a personal one with the same id.
 Every item in the note points back to where it sits in the raw, and nothing is added that the raw does not say. Another skill, such as a PRD you are writing, can pass it an input and link the note it gets back.

**Output:** the original, kept unchanged, in `{output_folder}/raw/` unless it is already in the project, and the note in the folder the calling skill names, else `{output_folder}/notes/`. Change either with `bmad-customize`.

## BMad Method Skills

The BMad Method module adds the six agents above and these workflow skills. The linked page covers when to use the skill and what it produces.

| Skill                           | Purpose                                                                                           | See                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bmad-agent-pm`                 | John, the Product Manager: create, update, or validate a PRD or another planning document        | [Define Requirements and a Specification](../plan/define-requirements-and-a-specification.md)          |
| `bmad-ux`                       | Capture the UX vision as `DESIGN.md` and `EXPERIENCE.md`                                          | [Design UX and Architecture](../plan/design-ux-and-architecture.md)                                    |
| `bmad-architecture`             | Record the architecture decisions that keep separately built parts consistent                     | [Design UX and Architecture](../plan/design-ux-and-architecture.md)                                    |
| `bmad-project-context`          | Set up, refresh, or audit the repository's agent instructions                                     | [Set and Maintain Project Context](../existing-codebases/set-and-maintain-project-context.md)          |
| `bmad-build`                    | Turn a work item into working code, reviewed and verified                                         | [Build a Change](../build/build-a-change.md)                                                           |
| `bmad-build-auto`               | Run one iteration of an unattended development loop                                               | [Autonomous Development Loops](../build/autonomous-development-loops.md)                               |
| `bmad-code-review`              | Review code changes with several independent reviewers, then triage the findings                  | [Review a Change](../build/review-a-change.md)                                                         |
| `bmad-walkthrough`              | Guide a human review of a commit, PR, file, or directory, one block at a time                      | [Walk Through a Change](../build/walk-through-a-change.md)                                             |
| `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests`    | Generate automated API and end-to-end tests for implemented features                              | [Test Completed Work](../build/test-completed-work.md)                                                 |
| `bmad-retrospective`            | Review a completed epic against its evidence and decide whether to accept it                      | [Finish an Epic](../build/finish-an-epic.md)                                                           |

## Toolsmith Skills

The Toolsmith module is for authoring skills and is installed separately. See [Toolsmith](../toolsmith/toolsmith.md).

| Skill | Purpose | See |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `bmad-toolsmith` | Smithy, who builds and maintains skills, agents, and modules | [Toolsmith](../toolsmith/toolsmith.md) |
| `bmad-eval` | Measure whether a skill works with baseline, variant, quality, and trigger runs | [Eval Runner](../toolsmith/bmad-eval.md) |

## Deprecated Names

Earlier skill IDs, such as `bmad-create-prd`, `bmad-edit-prd`, `bmad-market-research`, `bmad-generate-project-context`, and `bmad-checkpoint-preview`, still resolve as forwarders to the current skill. Use the current names in new work.

## Naming and Modules

Every skill shipped by the bmad-code-org uses the `bmad-` prefix followed by a descriptive name: `bmad-agent-dev`, `bmad-ux`, `bmad-build`. A custom module uses its own code as the prefix; see [Add Modules](../customize/add-modules.md) and [Modules and Registration](../toolsmith/modules.md).

## Troubleshooting

**Skills not appearing after install.** Some platforms require skills to be enabled in settings. Check your tool's documentation, then restart it or reload the window.

**Expected skills are missing.** The skills CLI installs only the skills you named. Run the module's install again, for example `npx skills add bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/skills/method --skill '*'`, or add the missing ones by name with `--skill`, then `bmad setup`, and check that the skill directories exist.

**Skills from a removed module still appear.** The installer does not delete old skill directories. Remove the stale directories, or delete the whole skills directory and re-run the installer for a clean set.
docs/plan/break-work-into-stories-and-tr:
---
title: 'Break Work into Stories and Track It'
description: Turn intent or a PRD into ticket entries, build them directly, and track progress in joined plans.
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

Ask Sofia, the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`), to split and track work. She accepts described intent or a PRD, writes the requirements into the initiative or epic file, and slices from them. One small story or bug can go straight to [Build](../build/build-a-change.md) without ticketing.

## Plan the Work

For several epics, create an initiative and ask Sofia to slice it. Each epic starts as a thin envelope, marked `refined: false`: its outcome, boundaries, and done-when checks as far as they are known, with no requirements yet. Ask Sofia to refine an epic before its stories are planned. She says what is already settled, names each open point with her pick (settle it now, spike it, or leave it to the stories), and writes its requirements. You can flesh it out further with a PRD, UX, architecture, or research run on the epic itself. Then incept the epic to propose its stories and bugs in build order, with requirement coverage, dependencies, and verification. Review the breakdown before accepting it.

The initiative's `tickets/tickets.toml` lists epics, each in its own folder beside that file. Each epic's `tickets/tickets.toml` lists entries with stable ids. A planned entry needs no story file. Standalone tracked stories and bugs have files in `backlog/`; they do not need an invented epic. Work bigger than one initiative goes under a parent initiative, whose `tickets/tickets.toml` lists child initiatives instead of epics.

See [Set Up the Ticket Tree](./set-up-the-ticket-tree.md) for store and tracker configuration.

## Build an Entry

Say “build story 1.2” to `bmad-build`. It reads the entry and epic, plus an existing refined leaf file, and writes acceptance criteria into its plan. Refinement before building is optional unless the work needs it.

The plan sits beside the epic's `tickets.toml`, in its `tickets/` folder, as `story-<slug>-plan.md`. Its numeric `ticket` joins the entry. A backlog plan uses its leaf file stem instead. The plan owns status and records the baseline before changes.

For unattended work, explicitly dispatch a ticket to `bmad-build-auto`, one invocation per ticket. It does not select the next ticket itself. Read [Autonomous Development Loops](../build/autonomous-development-loops.md) before wiring a runner.

## Track Progress

Ask Sofia “what's next?” or “show status.” Plans carry build progress. A build finishes at `built`, shown in the review column; the user or orchestrator decides when to mark it `done`. A tracker card's status remains separate from build status.

Keep completed plans. Deleting one removes the state and evidence later builds, review, and retrospective read.

## Review and Close

`bmad-code-review` reads a ticket's plan and baseline and appends a dated `Code Review` block. It never changes ticket status. When the epic is finished, run [Retrospective](../build/finish-an-epic.md) with its folder, id, or slug. Retrospective writes its evidence and verdict in the epic folder, beside the epic file; Sofia handles confirmed closure.

## Replan

Tell Sofia when a requirement, architecture choice, or dependency changes significantly: “this changed, what now.” She names the change and the ticket it lands on, reads that ticket, its memlog, its breakdown, and the finished children, and says whether what is required changed or only how it is delivered. When what is required changed, she updates the ticket's requirements first, keeping ids stable and naming the entries that went stale. Then she re-slices the affected epics, drops what no longer belongs, and records the reason as a dated `Decision:` line in each container's Notes. There is no proposal file, and nothing already built is rewritten.
docs/plan/choose-a-planning-path.md:
---
title: 'Choose a Planning Path'
description: Choose the smallest BMad path that safely fits a software change, from a trivial edit to a multi-epic project.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

Use this page to decide how much planning a change needs. The answer turns on
one question: is the intent already well defined? If it is, give it to Sofia,
the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`), who writes the ticket's requirements at
the size of the work, and build. If it is not,
the other pages in this chapter are how you get a defined intent. If the work
belongs to an organization, with a PRD other people must approve and several
engineers building in parallel, read
[Plan Inside an Organization](./plan-inside-an-organization.md) first; it
says how this chapter fits the process you already have.

## Start from the Intent

A well-defined intent says what should be true when the work is done, what
must not change, and what is out of scope: complete enough that someone else
could build it without guessing, and no longer than that. Where it came from
does not matter: a sentence, an issue, a forged idea, a research report, a
PRD.

Keep the input short. Sofia reads everything you give her in one pass,
and the practical ceiling is a few tens of thousands of tokens, roughly a
40-page document. Hand her a pile of raw documents several times that size and
she silently loses the parts that mattered; condense them first. If Sofia
says the input is too thin, you are not done on this chapter yet.

- **Well-defined intent**: give it to Sofia. Work that fits one Build
  session goes straight to `bmad-build`; for epic-sized work she fills the
  epic's requirements, then slices it into stories, then a Build per story. See
  [Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md).
- **Anything else**: the intent is not ready yet. Use the pages below until it
  is, then give it to Sofia. She writes the requirements; she does not
  help you figure out what you want.

If the change fits one implementation session, you are on the Build page's
territory, not this chapter's: [Build a Change](../build/build-a-change.md)
covers sizing a session and whether a small change needs BMad at all.

:::note[Prerequisites]
Install BMad before using Build or another BMad workflow. You don't need BMad
for an obvious, low-risk edit.
:::

## Get to a Well-Defined Intent

These are independent tools, not stages. Pick the ones the gap calls for, in
any order. None of them build anything. Condense what they produce and hand
Sofia the result, not the raw pile.

| The intent is missing                                            | Do this                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A clear idea at all, or confidence the idea is good              | [Explore and Validate an Idea](./explore-and-validate-an-idea.md)                                            |
| Evidence a decision should rest on                               | [Research a Decision](./research-a-decision.md)                                                              |
| A written account of what the product is, for a PRD or a pitch   | A brief or PRFAQ: [Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md)    |
| Shared decisions several epics or agents must follow             | [Design UX and Architecture](./design-ux-and-architecture.md)                                                |
| Agreement, ownership, and sign-off among several people or teams | A PRD as the document the organization owns: [Plan Inside an Organization](./plan-inside-an-organization.md) |

A short list of decisions is often enough on its own. You need a PRD when more
than one person must agree on what the product is, or more than one epic must
not diverge; otherwise skip it. A multi-epic product gives those documents to
Sofia once, at the initiative; each epic's requirements are cut from the
initiative's lines.

## Planning Skills and What They Produce

Every skill in this chapter writes a document you can hand on. The table runs from analysis through planning to solutioning; each chapter page is linked from the first skill it covers and explains when its skills fit. In an installed project, `bmad` recommends the next one. Each document lands in its own `<type>-<slug>/` folder inside the active initiative's folder, or directly in the output folder (`_bmad-output` by default) when no initiative is active. A document from John, or a `bmad-ux` or `bmad-architecture` run, on an epic lands in that epic's folder instead.

| Skill                           | Purpose                                                                                                                                        | Produces                                                                            |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bmad-brainstorming`            | Generate ideas with a facilitated session ([Explore and Validate an Idea](./explore-and-validate-an-idea.md))                                  | `brainstorm.html` keepsake plus an optional `brainstorm-<topic>.md`                 |
| `bmad-forge-idea`               | Pressure-test an idea until it hardens, proves out, or dies cheaply                                                                            | `forge-report.html` every run; `forge-<slug>.md` when the idea hardens              |
| `bmad-deep-recon`               | Research a subject to support a decision ([Research a Decision](./research-a-decision.md))                                                     | Cited `research-<topic>.md` plus an optional HTML briefing                          |
| `bmad-agent-analyst`            | Mary, the Business Analyst: write a brief when the concept is clear, stress-test it customer-first with a PRFAQ, or write a BRD ([Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md)) | `brief-<slug>.md`, `prfaq-<slug>.md` or `brd-<slug>.md`, `.memlog.md`              |
| `bmad-agent-pm`                 | John, the Product Manager: create, update, or validate a PRD or another planning document                                                                                 | Create/update: `<id>-<slug>.md` (such as `prd-<slug>.md`), `.memlog.md`, optional HTML view; validate: `review-*.md` findings |
| `bmad-ux`                       | Record how the product looks and behaves ([Design UX and Architecture](./design-ux-and-architecture.md))                                       | `DESIGN.md`, `EXPERIENCE.md`, `ux-<slug>.md`, `.memlog.md`                          |
| `bmad-architecture`             | Make the technical decisions that keep separately built parts consistent                                                                       | `architecture-<slug>.md` by default                                                 |
| `bmad-agent-po` | Sofia, the Product Owner: write a ticket's requirements from any input, then [plan and track entries](./break-work-into-stories-and-track-it.md) | Requirements and Constraints in the initiative, epic, or story file, `.memlog.md` beside it, ordered `tickets.toml`, and optional leaf files |

John (`bmad-agent-pm`) creates, updates, and validates twelve planning documents;
the work's altitude picks which, and he names close alternatives. A brief from
Mary feeds the PRD, which John reads during discovery, but neither requires the other.

A business requirements document (`brd`) fits only when the people who want the system and the people who build it are separate parties, such as a client and a vendor, or when a regulator or contract expects a signed baseline. Mary writes it, the sponsor signs it, and John's PRD or SRS picks up its ids. Other product work inside one organization skips it.

![Three columns of planning skills and the files each writes: analysis (brainstorming, forge idea, deep recon, and Mary for a brief, PRFAQ or BRD), planning (John for a PRD or other planning document, and UX), and solutioning (architecture and Sofia, the Product Owner), all handing off to bmad-build, one session per unit](/diagrams/planning-skills.svg)

## Size Follows the Intent

The size of the intent decides how many Build sessions follow. One coherent
outcome that needs several sessions is an epic. Work that spans several epics,
or likely needs roughly 20 or more sessions, is a project. Scope is only one
signal: use more planning when the work has high risk, unclear requirements,
broad architectural reach, cross-system effects, or coordination between
people or teams.

![Four nested paths reuse the same unit: edit directly, run one Build, repeat Build across an epic, or repeat epic paths across a project](/diagrams/development-paths.svg)

Every path uses the same implementation unit. Larger work adds shared context
around that unit and repeats it; it does not switch to a separate delivery
system.

## Run the Path

### 1. Start Epic-Sized Work

Use this path when the work needs several Build sessions but still has one
coherent outcome.

**Define and divide the epic**

1. Give Sofia the epic intent. She fills the epic's requirements from what
   you have, then slices. See
   [Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md)
   for what the requirements hold and when they are enough on their own.
2. She plans the epic with you and records the stories in build order in the
   epic's `tickets.toml`.
3. Review the proposed order and decide which stories need a checkpoint.
4. Build each story from its entry when you are ready; no story file is
   needed. Refine a story first only when its entry says `refine = true`, the
   ticket has no epic, or you want the acceptance criteria written before
   build.

The breakdown is an execution plan, not a promise that nothing will change.
Tell Sofia what changed, and she updates the requirements and re-slices the
remaining stories, when earlier work reveals a missing constraint, a better
division, or a conflict between stories.

**Establish the implementation pattern**

Implement important, risky, or foundational stories with `bmad-build`. Early
stories often settle the architecture, initial project structure, and repeated
patterns that later stories will follow. Give those decisions human attention
before automating repetitions of them.

Run Build once per story, naming the story. Build writes its plan beside the
epic's `tickets.toml` and leaves the plan at `built` until you mark it done
through Sofia. To run stories unattended instead, give
`bmad-build-auto` the story as its intent, one run per story; see
[Autonomous Development Loops](../build/autonomous-development-loops.md).

**Finish the epic**

Verify the stories together, then run `bmad-retrospective` with the epic folder, id, or slug. It reads entries and joined plans and judges the combined result against the epic's requirements. Keep those plans after closure.
See [Finish an Epic](../build/finish-an-epic.md).

### 2. Start Project-Sized Work

Use the full BMad flow for a greenfield product, a multi-epic initiative, or
work likely to need roughly 20 or more implementation sessions.

Prepare only the planning the project actually needs from the table above ([Plan Inside an Organization](./plan-inside-an-organization.md) covers who owns which document and where sign-off happens). Then give the documents to Sofia, who fills the initiative's requirements and slices it into epics. Each epic starts thin: before its stories are planned, ask Sofia to refine it. On a small initiative that is a single question; on a larger one she names what is still open, with her pick for each, and you can add a PRD, UX, architecture, or research run on the epic itself. Track the stories with [Break Work into Stories and Track It](./break-work-into-stories-and-track-it.md), and close each epic with [Finish an Epic](../build/finish-an-epic.md).

When the work is more than one initiative's worth, Sofia proposes a parent initiative that lists its child initiatives in build order. Each child is planned and built like any other initiative.

These documents coordinate implementation. They do not replace Build. Each
epic still becomes a sequence of one-session units. Independent epic streams
can proceed in parallel when their boundaries are explicit. Each stream needs
an owner, and all streams stay accountable to the same product intent and
architecture. Run integration checks and a retrospective at each epic
boundary.

Dividing work can lose information: a requirement weakens, a constraint
disappears, or two correct stories fail when combined. The PRD, architecture,
and each ticket's requirements exist so later sessions can still see the whole.

## After Decisions Stabilize

`bmad-build-auto` runs one session without waiting for human input. It does
not choose the next story or own the backlog. Use it after the important
implementation decisions are stable. For the worker contract, see
[Autonomous Development Loops](../build/autonomous-development-loops.md).

## What You Get

A path sized to the work: an epic with its requirements and stories, or shared
product documents plus an initiative sliced into epics for a project — each
still implemented one Build session at a time.
docs/plan/define-requirements-and-a-spec:
---
title: 'Define Requirements and a Specification'
description: Choose between writing a ticket's requirements with Sofia and the full product-planning path — product brief or PRFAQ, then a PRD — and know what each produces.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

Use this page to pick the requirements path for the work in front of you: a
product brief or a PRFAQ, then a PRD, for a product; or Sofia, the Product
Owner (`bmad-agent-po`), to write the ticket's requirements that
implementation reads.

## Which Path Applies

[Choose a Planning Path](./choose-a-planning-path.md) decides the size. Most
work goes straight to Sofia from whatever defined the intent: a forged idea,
a PRFAQ, a brainstorm intent, an issue. A PRD becomes necessary when
several people must agree on what the product is or several epics must stay
aligned; [Plan Inside an Organization](./plan-inside-an-organization.md)
covers that setting. This page covers what each document is for and which
skill writes it. None of them replaces the ticket's requirements: the
initiative, epic, or story file is the specification at its level, its
Requirements section is what Build reads, and when there is a PRD, that is
where those lines come from.

John's documents and the UX skill steer the same way. Each opens with a brain
dump: tell it everything and point it at any files you have. Then you choose a
working mode. **Fast path** batches the remaining gaps into a question or two
and drafts the whole document with `[ASSUMPTION]` tags for you to correct.
**Coaching path** pulls the thinking out of you section by section and pushes
back where an answer is thin. Sessions can be paused and resumed.

## Product Brief: Capture Conviction

Ask Mary, the Business Analyst (`bmad-agent-analyst`), to create, update, or validate a brief ("write a product brief"): a one- to
two-page account of the product concept, right-sized to its purpose. A passion
project does not get investor-grade rigor; a pitch input does. She reads
the stakes early and calibrates how hard she pushes.

Use it when your concept is relatively clear and you want it written down
before a PRD. It produces `brief-<slug>.md`, which John reads when he writes the PRD. For
serious market sizing or competitor teardowns, use
[Deep Recon](./research-a-decision.md).

## PRFAQ: Working Backwards

Ask Mary, the Business Analyst (`bmad-agent-analyst`), for Amazon's Working Backwards method as a challenge ("create a PRFAQ", "work backwards"). You write the press release announcing the finished product before anything is built, then answer the hardest questions customers and stakeholders would ask. Solution-first and technology-first openings get redirected to the customer's problem. Vague answers get challenged. When you are stuck she offers concrete alternatives rather than repeating the question.

The document has four parts: the press release; the customer FAQ; the internal FAQ on feasibility and trade-offs; and a verdict on the concept's strength, written last. Mary shows you the four parts first and takes them in order, finishing each before the next, and her role changes with the part: an editor for the press release, a skeptical customer for the customer FAQ, the stakeholder panel for the internal FAQ. Claims about the market and competitors are checked against current research, not assumed. If after a few exchanges you cannot name a customer or a problem, she sends you back to brainstorming or Forge Idea instead of forcing it.

Use it when you want the concept stress-tested before committing resources. If you cannot write a compelling press release, the product is not ready. It produces `prfaq-<slug>.md` and, beside it, the same document laid out as a press release page in HTML, and it runs headless for an unattended first draft when you say so and supply the customer, problem, stakes, and concept up front.

Brief and PRFAQ both feed a PRD, and the PRFAQ can feed Sofia directly when no PRD is needed. Choose by how much challenge you want: the brief is collaborative discovery, the PRFAQ is the harder path. Neither is required; John starts a PRD from a brain dump on his own.

## PRD: Agree on What and Why

Talk to John, the Product Manager (`bmad-agent-pm`), to create, update, or validate a Product Requirements Document. Ask for him by name or say what you want: "create a PRD", "update the PRD", "validate this PRD".

- **Create** runs discovery, then drafts. User journeys are told with a named
  protagonist.
- **Update** reconciles the PRD with a change signal, surfacing conflicts with
  earlier decisions before applying anything.
- **Validate** critiques without changing and writes the findings to
  `review-*.md` files beside the PRD.

The PRD describes capabilities, not implementation: features grouped, with
functional requirements under stable IDs and non-functional requirements in
their own section. Length scales with
stakes, from about two pages for a hobby project to as long as the
requirements need for a launch.

It answers "what should we build and why." It does not say how; that is
[Design UX and Architecture](./design-ux-and-architecture.md). It does not
divide work into stories; that is
[Break Work into Stories and Track It](./break-work-into-stories-and-track-it.md).
If you open with a one-pager in mind, John points you to Mary for the brief; an idea to vet
goes to her PRFAQ.

## Other Planning Documents

Besides the PRD, John writes a prototype plan, an experiment card, a light PRD for a very simple project, a spec for a coding agent, an opportunity assessment, a business case, a program charter, a strategy narrative, a Shape Up pitch, a requirements specification, and a launch plan. Mary writes the business requirements document that a PRD or requirements specification picks up when a separate party builds the work. The work's altitude picks the document: a program takes a charter or a strategy narrative, an epic a PRD or a pitch, and a feature outside the ticket tree a spec for a coding agent. He says why he chose it and names any close alternative, so you can switch. Each works like the PRD: fast or coaching path; create, update, or validate. The experiment card, opportunity assessment and pitch take their sections in order instead, because each step depends on the one before: a pitch fixes its appetite before the solution, and an experiment its thresholds before it runs. A pitch also gets a one-page HTML view for the betting table.

Your team can add its own planning documents, or replace or extend John's, with a file in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`. Doc standards, reviewers, output, style, and the HTML view are set on `bmad-facilitate`, the skill that runs John's documents. See [Write a Document Template](../customize/write-a-document-template.md).

## Requirements: The Contract Implementation Reads

Point Sofia at what you have: "distill this PRD", "write the requirements
from these notes", or `/bmad-agent-po <path>`. She writes the Requirements
and Constraints sections of the ticket's own file, the initiative, epic, or
story that is active or that you name. Each Requirements line says what is
possible and what shows it was met, under a stable `R<n>` id that names its
source: `R1 (FR-2, FR-5)` on an initiative, `R1 (parent R3)` on an epic. The
input's non-goals go to Boundaries and its open questions to Notes. Tables,
diagrams, glossaries, and documents other skills already wrote sit beside
the ticket or stay where they are; the ticket names them in References
rather than copying them.

Sofia writes the requirements; she does not help you figure out what you
want. Rich input is extracted with no questions. Sparse input gets a choice:
a best-effort draft where every gap becomes an open question, or a guided
walk through the sections. Input too thin to use ("an app for hikers") is
sent to John for a PRD. Input too large is the other failure: a few tens of
thousands of tokens is the practical ceiling, so condense a pile of material
first.

After every run she reports the ticket's path, the requirement count, the
companions, and the verdict of her own check, then lists the `Assumption:`
and `Open question:` lines for you to walk through. Resolving one can update
the source input, the ticket, or both; say which. Read the `R` lines
yourself: a line you would not defend to a stakeholder is one to change now,
before anything is cut from it.

Sofia is the only writer of the Requirements and Constraints sections. Do not
hand-edit them; she derives them from `.memlog.md` beside the ticket, so a
hand edit is overwritten on the next run. When the input changes, run her
again with the change and she updates the sections in place, keeps every `R`
id stable, and names the entries whose `covers` cite a changed id. The PRD,
UX, and architecture skills can run in any order and feed the same ticket.

When the ticket's lines read as several slices, she offers once to slice. To split at any time, say "slice this initiative", which cuts it into epics and writes each one thin; "refine this epic", which works out with you what its stories must agree on and writes its requirements; or "incept this epic", which plans one epic with you in build order and records the stories in the epic's `tickets.toml`, each citing the epic's `R` ids. A constraint or design decision that comes up while slicing goes back into the ticket's requirements as an update. See [Choose a Planning Path](./choose-a-planning-path.md#1-start-epic-sized-work) for how the epic then runs.

To run the planned stories unattended, explicitly dispatch each ticket to
[`bmad-build-auto`](../build/autonomous-development-loops.md) as `ticket <ref>`,
one run per ticket. No leaf file needs to be pulled first.

:::note[What each skill produces]
John (`bmad-agent-pm`): `<id>-<slug>.md`, such as `prd-<slug>.md` or
`business-case-<slug>.md`, or `review-*.md` findings.
Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`): `brief-<slug>.md`, `prfaq-<slug>.md` or `brd-<slug>.md`. Each document
lands in its own `<type>-<slug>/` folder in the active initiative's folder,
or in the output folder when no initiative is active. Sofia writes the
Requirements and Constraints sections of the initiative, epic, or story file,
with `.memlog.md` and any companions beside it. Exact paths and options
belong to each skill; see
[Planning Skills and What They Produce](./choose-a-planning-path.md#planning-skills-and-what-they-produce).
:::

## What Comes Next

With a PRD in hand for multi-epic work, decide whether the work needs shared
design decisions: [Design UX and Architecture](./design-ux-and-architecture.md).
With an epic's requirements written, ask Sofia to slice it and go to
[Break Work into Stories and Track It](./break-work-into-stories-and-track-it.md).
docs/plan/design-ux-and-architecture.md:
---
title: 'Design UX and Architecture'
description: When UX and architecture work is necessary, and how documented decisions stop agents and epics from implementing a system in conflicting ways.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

Use this page to decide whether a change needs UX or architecture work before
implementation. Most changes do not. Multi-epic and cross-system work usually
does, because without shared decisions each agent or session makes its own.

## Do You Need It?

| Work characteristics                              | Guidance                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Clear, local change with established patterns     | Usually unnecessary                                           |
| Several related components with known constraints | Optional, based on coordination risk                          |
| Multiple epics or cross-system decisions          | Needed to align implementation                                |
| Regulated, high-risk, or enterprise initiative    | Follow required governance; architecture is normally required |

If several epics could be implemented by different agents or people, you need
architecture. If the product has a user interface whose look and behavior
matter to the outcome, you need UX.

Both change what `bmad-build` reads; neither changes how Build runs. Build
still runs one session at a time. What changes is that each session reads the
same decisions, so the sessions fit together.

## The Problem Without Shared Decisions

When several agents implement different parts of a system with no shared
guidance, each makes independent technical choices. The results conflict in
predictable places: one epic exposes REST while another writes GraphQL;
`snake_case` columns meet `camelCase` ones; Redux in one area and React
Context in the next; different directory layouts and test patterns per epic;
session cookies here and JWT there. Each choice is defensible alone. Together
they produce integration issues discovered mid-sprint, rework, and
inconsistent patterns.

## The Architecture Spine

Run `bmad-architecture` and you get a short architecture document (the
**spine**). It records only the decisions that would conflict if two people
made them independently: the design approach, the boundaries, how state is
changed, who owns shared data. The stack, the folder tree, and the full data
shape are starting points; the code owns them once they exist.

One test decides what belongs. If two units built this independently, could
they choose incompatibly? A decision goes in the spine only when the answer
is yes, the call is non-obvious, and it is a real trade-off. Everything else
is left to the code. Each decision gets a stable ID so tickets and stories can
cite it.

The skill works from the ticket's requirements, with whatever else you have beside
them: a long architecture document to shorten, or an existing codebase, where it
reads the real code and records the conventions already there. Coaching is the default:
the important calls are shown with the alternatives weighed, then you choose.
A Fast path drafts the whole spine with `[ASSUMPTION]` tags instead. For a
new project it recommends a current, well-known starter, because a good one
already decides a lot of the architecture.

Point it at the whole system or at one epic; an epic spine inherits the parent's decisions, records only what the parent left open, and is written in the epic's folder. When Sofia refines an epic, she reminds you that an epic run is one way to flesh it out. When the architecture skill finishes, it offers to add the spine to the ticket's References through Sofia, the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`), which is how Build and the readiness gate find it. Seed [project context](../existing-codebases/set-and-maintain-project-context.md) from it so every later skill reads the same rules.

:::caution[Common mistakes]
Deciding the API style "as we go", documenting every minor choice, and a spine
written once and never updated are the three ways this step fails. Document
decisions that cross epic boundaries, keep the spine current as you learn, and
tell Sofia when a significant mid-implementation change arrives.
:::

## UX Design

Run `bmad-ux` when user experience matters to the outcome. It produces two
peer documents: `DESIGN.md` for how the product looks (colors, typography,
spacing, components) and `EXPERIENCE.md` for how it works (information
architecture, behavior and states, accessibility, key user flows). Both win
over any mock or wireframe on conflict.

The facilitator records your vision; it never volunteers colors, patterns, or directions. Three working modes: a Fast path that drafts both documents with `[ASSUMPTION]` tags, a Coaching path that walks the decisions with creative tools (color themes, design directions, wireframes, key-screen mocks), or a design handoff that builds a prompt for an external design tool and folds its output back in. UX can lead the PRD, follow it, or stand alone. Run on one epic, when the initiative's UX does not cover its screens, it writes in the epic's folder.

Skip it for back-end work, internal tooling with no real interface, and
changes to an existing UI that already has established patterns.

## What Comes Next

The spine and the UX documents become References of the ticket and input to
[Break Work into Stories and Track It](./break-work-into-stories-and-track-it.md),
where the readiness gate checks that stories do not depend on decisions
nothing records.
docs/plan/explore-and-validate-an-idea.m:
---
title: 'Explore and Validate an Idea'
description: Decide which early idea skill to use — generate options with brainstorming, pressure-test a held idea with Forge Idea, or skip idea work and go straight to requirements.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

Use this page to decide what to do with an idea before you commit to
requirements or code. Idea work is optional. Skipping it is fine when you
already know what you want; skipping it on a vague idea means every later
document inherits the vagueness.

## Pick a Starting Point

Start from your situation, not from a preferred skill.

| Situation                                                         | Use                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "I have a topic and want far more ideas on it than I'd get alone" | `bmad-brainstorming`                                                                                          |
| "I hold an idea and want it clarified, tested, or made better"    | `bmad-forge-idea`                                                                                             |
| "I need to understand the market, domain, or technology first"    | `bmad-deep-recon` — see [Research a Decision](./research-a-decision.md)                                       |
| "I already have conviction and want it written down"              | A product brief — see [Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md) |
| "I have a product concept and want it proven customer-first"      | A PRFAQ — see [Define Requirements and a Specification](./define-requirements-and-a-specification.md)         |
| "I want my agents to discuss or decide together"                  | `bmad-party-mode` — see [Run Multi-Agent Discussions](../customize/run-multi-agent-discussions.md)            |

None of these are stages. Run whichever fit, in any order, and condense what
comes out before the next step.

:::tip[Not Sure?]
Run `bmad` and describe your situation. It recommends a starting point
based on what you have already produced.
:::

## Generate Options with Brainstorming

Run `bmad-brainstorming` when you have a topic and want to push past the
obvious ideas on it. You choose the stance for the session:

- **Facilitator**: the coach never supplies ideas. It runs techniques and asks
  sharper questions so every idea is yours.
- **Creative Partner**: it facilitates and plays along, trading ideas with you.
- **Ideate for me**: it runs the whole session itself and shows you the result.

Tell it what you are brainstorming and why; the goal shapes which techniques
it offers. You pick a batch of techniques, or let it choose, and it runs each
until it stops producing, aiming well past a hundred ideas before it lets you
wrap. Say when you want to narrow and it switches to prioritizing and
deciding. Sessions can be paused and resumed.

You get an HTML record of the session, and a short `brainstorm-<topic>.md`
holding only the chosen discoveries, shaped to feed Sofia, the Product Owner
