| Game Dev Studio, code `gds` | Game design documents and game-aware planning for Unity, Unreal, Godot, and custom engines | [bmad-module-game-dev-studio](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio) |

Each repository's README says which BMad version it supports. TEA's `bmad-tea-automate` generates heavier test coverage than the built-in `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests`; [Test Completed Work](../build/test-completed-work.md) helps you choose between them.

## Add a module

From your project folder, add the module's skills with the Skills CLI. For TEA:

```bash
npx skills add bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise
```

Select your coding tool and the skills you want. Include the module record, `bmod-tea` here. Keep the project and global installation scopes consistent with the rest of your BMad skills.

Then ask the `bmad` skill to run `bmad setup tea`. Setup asks the module's configuration questions, places its scripts under `_bmad/<code>/`, and offers any migration the module ships. Ask for `bmad status` to confirm the module and its version.

Any repository that follows the module layout installs the same way. The source can be a local folder, or a repository at a tag, as in `owner/repo#v1.2.0`.

## Keep a module updated

`bmad setup` compares each module's version with its source and offers to run `npx skills update` when a newer one exists. If you update by hand, run `bmad setup` afterwards.

When a newer version exists for a module installed from a tag, `bmad status` reports `pinned`, because `npx skills update` keeps it on that tag. It also gives the `npx skills add owner/repo#<tag> --skill …` command that moves the module record and its skills to the newer tag.

## Create your own module

Ask Smithy, the `bmad-toolsmith` skill, to scaffold a module, add skills and agents to it, and validate it. [Toolsmith](../toolsmith/toolsmith.md) describes what it builds and how.

A module needs a `bmod-<code>` record folder holding a `bmod.toml`, a stub `SKILL.md`, and a `help/help.md` that `bmad` reads to guide users. Each of its skills carries a small `bmod.toml` that names the record. A module of one skill needs no record folder: that skill's own `bmod.toml` holds both tables, and its `help/`, `doc-templates/` and `roster.toml` sit in the skill folder. Founder is built this way. A repository with several modules gives each one its own folder under `skills/`, so `npx skills add owner/repo/skills/<code>` installs one whole. Publish the repository and others add it with `npx skills add`. To test before publishing, add it from the local folder.

## Modules in v6.12

v6.12 reads modules from the official list in `npx bmad-method install`, or from a Git URL or local path you give it:

| Input | Example |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS or SSH Git URL | `https://github.com/org/repo`, `git@github.com:org/repo.git` |
| URL with a subfolder or `@ref` | `https://github.com/org/repo/tree/main/my-module`, `https://github.com/org/repo@v1.2.0` |
| Local path | `/Users/me/projects/my-module` |

Pass a source on the command line with `--custom-source`; separate several sources with commas.

```bash
npx bmad-method install --directory . --custom-source /path/to/my-module --tools claude-code --yes
```

A source with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` lists its plugins for you to pick from. Without one, the installer scans the folder for skills and treats them as one module. Quick update (`--action quick-update`) refreshes installed modules from their recorded sources, and a full update (`--action update`) lets you add or remove them.
---
title: 'Adopt BMad Across a Team'
description: Recipes that make every developer's BMad follow your organization's rules, tools, templates, and agent roster — without forking a skill.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

You lead a team and want every developer's BMad to use the same tools,
follow the same conventions, publish to the same systems, and know the same
people. Each recipe below is one override file under `_bmad/custom/`,
committed to the repository so everyone inherits it on pull.

Pick the surface this way:

- The rule applies wherever an engineer does dev work: customize the **dev agent**.
- The rule applies only to one workflow, such as writing a product brief: customize **that workflow**.
- The change alters who is on the roster, or a path the whole team shares: edit **central config**.

For how override files merge with the shipped defaults, see
[Customize BMad](./customize-bmad.md). This page never repeats those
mechanics; it shows what to write.

:::tip[Applying these recipes]
Run the `bmad-customize` skill and describe the intent; it writes the
override file for recipes 1 through 3 and 6 and verifies the merge. Recipe
4 is a template file you copy and edit; recipe 5, the agent roster in central config, is hand-authored.
:::

Every per-skill recipe has a team form and a personal form. `bmad-agent-dev.toml`
is committed to git and applies to the whole team; `bmad-agent-dev.user.toml`
is gitignored and layers personal preferences on top. The same split holds
for every skill file and for central config.

## Recipe 1: Shape an agent across every workflow it dispatches

**File and key:** `_bmad/custom/bmad-agent-dev.toml`, `[agent] persistent_facts`.

Use this to standardize tool use and external systems for all dev work.
One file applies to every workflow the agent runs — build, code review,
test generation — and every engineer who pulls the repo inherits it.

**Example:** Amelia always uses Context7 for library docs and falls back to
Linear when a ticket is not in the ticket tree.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-agent-dev.toml

[agent]

persistent_facts = [
  "For any library documentation lookup (React, TypeScript, Zod, Prisma, etc.), call the context7 MCP tool (`mcp__context7__resolve_library_id` then `mcp__context7__get_library_docs`) before relying on training-data knowledge. Up-to-date docs trump memorized APIs.",
  "When a ticket reference cannot be resolved in the ticket tree, search Linear via `mcp__linear__search_issues` using the story ID or title before asking the user to clarify. If Linear returns a match, treat it as the authoritative story source.",
]
```

## Recipe 2: Enforce conventions inside one workflow

**File and key:** `_bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml`, `[workflow] persistent_facts`; for one document type, a file in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/` that extends its template.

Use this when the rule shapes the content of a workflow's output — for compliance, audit, or a downstream consumer — and should not follow the agent into other work. `bmad-facilitate` runs every document John (`bmad-agent-pm`) and Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`) write, so a fact on it reaches all of them; a `file:` entry loads a conventions document you already maintain.

**Example:** every planning document follows the organization's publishing conventions.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]

persistent_facts = [
  "file:{project-root}/docs/enterprise/publishing-conventions.md",
]
```

The facts load before the engine drafts, so the conventions are known in time.

A rule for one document type goes in an extension of its template, so it does not reach the others. Every product brief carries compliance fields. A section an extension adds is required unless its comment says optional, and its comment says where it goes:

```markdown
---
extends: brief
---

<!-- inputs: The owner, the target release and the security review status; only the user knows them. -->

## Compliance
<!-- After Scope. Owner, target release and security review status. -->
```

## Recipe 3: Publish completed output to external systems

**File and key:** `_bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml`, `[workflow] on_complete`.

Use this to send finished output to an external system (Confluence, Notion,
SharePoint) and open follow-up work (Jira, Linear, Asana). `on_complete` is
the right hook because it runs exactly once, after the workflow's output is
written; `activation_steps_append` runs on every activation, before the
work starts.

**Example:** planning documents publish to Confluence and offer an optional Jira epic.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]

on_complete = """
Publish and offer follow-up:

1. Read the document's file path from the prior step. If its frontmatter `status` is not `final`, stop and tell the user which open question blocks publication.
2. Call `mcp__atlassian__confluence_create_page` with:
   - space: "PRODUCT"
   - parent: "Planning"
   - title: the document's title
   - body: the document's markdown contents
   Capture the returned page URL.
3. Tell the user: "Published to Confluence: <url>".
4. Ask: "Want me to open a Jira epic for this now?"
5. If yes, call `mcp__atlassian__jira_create_issue` with:
   - type: "Epic"
   - project: "PROD"
   - summary: the document's title
   - description: a short summary plus a link back to the Confluence page.
   Report the epic key and URL.
6. If no, exit cleanly.

If either MCP tool fails, report the failure, print the document's path,
and ask the user to publish manually.
"""
```

Publishing to Confluence does not change anyone else's work, so it runs
without asking. Creating a Jira epic is visible to the team, so confirm
first. If a tool fails, give the user the file path instead of dropping
the output.

## Recipe 4: Swap in your own output template

**File:** a template in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/` with the shipped template's id.

Use this when the shipped structure does not match the format your organization expects. `bmad-facilitate` searches that folder first and the installed modules last, so a file there with the same `template:` id replaces the shipped one for John, Mary and anyone who calls the engine directly.

Copy the shipped brief from `bmad-agent-analyst/assets/template-brief.md` in your skills folder, with `brief-view.html` beside it, which its `view` names. Keep `template: brief` and the other frontmatter keys, and edit the copy. Here the description changes:

```markdown
---
title: ""
template: brief
version: 1.0.0
description: "Why to build it, in the format the steering committee reads."
status: draft
created: ""
updated: ""
---
```

The folder versions alongside the override files. When several teams share one repository, each can add its own folder to `template_libraries` from `bmad-facilitate.user.toml` without touching the committed file. To add rules without copying the template, extend it instead (recipe 2). See [Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md).

## Recipe 5: Customize the agent roster

**File:** `_bmad/custom/config.toml` (team) or `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` (personal).

Use central config to change who roster-driven skills (`bmad-party-mode`,
`bmad-retrospective`, `bmad-advanced-elicitation`) see, and to pin setup
answers the whole team shares. Per-skill files shape how one agent behaves
when it activates; central config shapes what other skills see when they
look at the roster. See
[Central configuration](./customize-bmad.md#central-configuration) for the
file layout.

### 5a. Rebrand an agent for the whole team

**Key:** `[agents.bmad-agent-analyst] description`.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.toml (committed — applies to every developer)

[agents.bmad-agent-analyst]
description = "Mary the Regulatory-Aware Business Analyst — channels Porter and Minto, but lives and breathes FDA audit trails. Speaks like a forensic investigator presenting a case file."
```

Party mode introduces Mary with the new description. It does not change
how she works when she activates; that still comes from her `[agent]`
override, as in recipe 1.

### 5b. Add a fictional agent

**Key:** `[agents.<code>]` with a `team` value.

A full descriptor is enough for roster features; no skill folder is
needed. Personal files suit this, since a cast is a matter of taste.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.user.toml (personal — gitignored)

[agents.spock]
team = "startrek"
name = "Commander Spock"
title = "Science Officer"
icon = "🖖"
description = "Logic first, emotion suppressed. Begins observations with 'Fascinating.' Never rounds up. Counterpoint to any argument that relies on gut instinct."

[agents.mccoy]
team = "startrek"
name = "Dr. Leonard McCoy"
title = "Chief Medical Officer"
icon = "⚕️"
description = "Country doctor's warmth, short fuse. 'Dammit Jim, I'm a doctor not a ___.' Ethics-driven counterweight to Spock."
```

Ask party mode to "invite the Enterprise crew": it filters by
`team = "startrek"` and includes Spock and McCoy. You can include real
BMad agents in the same party.

### 5c. Pin team settings

**Key:** `[core] output_folder`.

When the team needs one answer for a setting such as where BMad writes its
output, pin it here; it overrides `_bmad/config.toml`, and a developer's own
`_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` still wins over it. `output_folder` holds every initiative folder, the ticket tree, and
`backlog/`, so pinning it moves all of them together.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.toml

[core]
output_folder = "{project-root}/shared/bmad-output"
```

Personal settings stay in each developer's own
`_bmad/custom/config.user.toml`; the team file should not set them.

## Reinforce global rules in your IDE's session file

BMad customizations load when a skill activates. Most IDE tools also load
a global instruction file at the start of every session, before any skill
runs: `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.cursor/rules/`, or
`.github/copilot-instructions.md`. For a rule that should hold in a plain
chat with no skill active, restate it there too, if it is short enough to
repeat.

**Example:** one line in the repository's `CLAUDE.md` reinforcing the
dev-agent rule from recipe 1.

```markdown
Look up library docs through the context7 MCP tool (`mcp__context7__resolve_library_id` then `mcp__context7__get_library_docs`) before relying on training-data knowledge.
```

Each layer owns its own scope:

| Layer | Scope | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| IDE session file (`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`) | Every session, before any skill activates | Short, universal rules that should survive outside BMad |
| BMad agent customization | Every workflow the agent dispatches | Agent-specific behavior |
| BMad workflow customization | One workflow run | Output shape, publishing hooks, templates |
| BMad central config | Agent roster and shared settings | Who is on the roster and which paths the team shares |

Keep the IDE file short. The model reads it every turn.

## Recipe 6: Advanced fields

**File and keys:** `_bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml`, `[workflow] external_sources`,
`external_handoffs`, and `doc_standards`; template files in
`_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`.

Some workflows expose more fields than recipes 1 through 5 use. Check a
workflow's `customize.toml` to see which of these it has; the examples use
`bmad-facilitate`, which runs every document John (`bmad-agent-pm`) writes, so
its settings apply to his documents too. The same pattern applies wherever a
field appears.

### On-demand knowledge sources

`external_sources` connects the workflow to internal knowledge bases,
competitive databases, or compliance references. The agent consults them
only when the conversation surfaces a matching need, never preemptively.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]
external_sources = [
  "When the user mentions a competitor or market segment, query corp:competitive_db (category={project_name}) before drafting the differentiation section.",
  "For regulatory domains (healthcare, fintech, education), consult corp:compliance_reference before drafting domain-specific sections.",
]
```

Each entry names the MCP tool, the trigger, and the fields the tool needs.
If the tool is unavailable at runtime, the workflow falls back to standard
behavior and notes the gap.

### Automatic output publishing

`external_handoffs` sends finished artifacts to an external system after
the workflow finalizes. Unlike `on_complete` (recipe 3), it is an append
array: team entries stack, and each handoff fires independently.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]
external_handoffs = [
  "After finalize, upload the document to Confluence via corp:confluence_upload (space_key='PROD', parent_page='Planning'). Capture and surface the returned page URL.",
  "Mirror to Notion via notion:create_page (database_id='abc123', title=the document's title).",
]
```

If a named tool is unavailable, that handoff is skipped and flagged; the
local files always exist.

### Finalize-time doc standards

At finalize, after the content is complete and before the user sees it,
`doc_standards` applies your writing standards to the document.
Each entry is a `skill:`, `file:`, or plain-text directive; the passes run
in declared order within a document. It is an append array, so your entries
stack on the workflow's shipped default
(`skill:bmad-review lenses=structure,prose`). Put broad structural passes
before narrow prose passes.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]
doc_standards = [
  "file:{project-root}/docs/enterprise/voice-and-tone.md",
  "All dates must use ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD).",
  "Replace any use of 'leverage' with 'use'.",
]
```

### Template libraries and extensions

John and `bmad-facilitate` change templates the same way: put a file in
`_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`. A new `template:` id adds a template, and a
shipped id replaces it. To swap in a regulated-industry PRD, save it there with
`template: prd` and a `rubric:` beside it. A file with `extends:` adds your
rules without copying the template, so updates to the original still reach you:

```markdown
---
extends: business-case
---

<!-- done when: Every cost line names its source. -->

## Budget Owner
<!-- required, after the cost section. The budget owner and cost center. -->
```

The template file format and extensions are in
[Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md).

## Combining recipes

All six recipes compose. One workflow file can set `persistent_facts`
(recipe 2) and `on_complete` (recipe 3), with your template beside it in `facilitate-templates/` (recipe 4); the
agent-wide rule (recipe 1) lives in a separate file under the agent's
name; central config (recipe 5) pins the roster and shared paths; advanced
fields (recipe 6) add sources and handoffs. Every layer applies.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml (workflow)

[workflow]
persistent_facts = ["..."]
on_complete = """ ... """
```

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-agent-analyst.toml (agent — Mary dispatches the brief)

[agent]
persistent_facts = ["Always include a 'Regulatory Review' section when the domain involves healthcare, finance, or children's data."]
```

Mary loads the regulatory-review rule when she activates. When the user
asks her for a brief, the engine adds your conventions,
writes to your template, and publishes to Confluence on
completion. For planning with several people or teams, see
[Plan Inside an Organization](../plan/plan-inside-an-organization.md).

## Troubleshooting

**Override not taking effect?** Check that the file is under
`_bmad/custom/` with the exact skill directory name (`bmad-agent-dev.toml`,
not `bmad-dev.toml`). See
[Customize BMad](./customize-bmad.md#troubleshooting) for the rest.

**MCP tool name unknown?** Use the exact name the MCP server exposes in the
current session; ask your IDE assistant to list the available MCP tools.
A name written into `persistent_facts` or `on_complete` does nothing if
that server is not connected.

---
title: 'Customize a Document for Your Team'
description: Make every PRD ask the questions your company cares about, then give one department a PRD of its own.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

Make John's PRD ask the questions your company cares about, without touching BMad's own files, so every PRD your team writes covers them. Then give one department a PRD of its own when its needs outgrow the shared one.

## What You'll Learn

- Add a required section with its own coaching
- Change how the coach works an existing section
- See exactly what the coach read for a run
- Choose between extending a template, replacing it and making a new one

:::note[Prerequisites]
BMad installed with the BMad Method module, `bmad setup` run, and a coding tool open in your project. See [Install BMad](../start/install-bmad.md).
:::

:::tip[Quick Path]
Tell `bmad-customize` what every PRD needs. It writes an extension in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/` and shows you the result. Write a PRD with John and open `.template.md` in its folder to see your rules in what the coach read.
:::

## The Example

Larkspur, a fictional company, sells appointment scheduling software to clinics. Two things went wrong last quarter. A reminders feature launched while Support had no answers ready, and tickets tripled in the first week. And PRDs kept promising metrics nobody tracks, so no one could say whether a launch worked.

Larkspur's product lead wants two changes to every PRD:

| Change | Kind | What the coach does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A **Support readiness** section | A new section | Asks who leads Support for the launch and which questions customers will ask first, and refuses "Support will figure it out" |
| **Success metrics** taken from the company's metrics catalog | A change to a section John's PRD already has | Reads the catalog before asking, and logs an open question instead of inventing a metric |

## Step 1: Give the Coach a Catalog to Read

The metrics rule points at a file your team keeps. For this tutorial, create `docs/metrics-catalog.md` with a few rows:

```markdown
# Metrics catalog

| Metric | Definition | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No-show rate | Booked appointments with no check-in, per week | Clinic Analytics |
| Reminder delivery rate | Reminders delivered over reminders sent | Messaging |
| Tickets per 100 clinics | Support tickets opened per 100 active clinics, per week | Support Ops |
```

## Step 2: Ask bmad-customize for the Change

Run the `bmad-customize` skill and say what you want in plain words:

```text
Every PRD at Larkspur needs a Support readiness section after MVP scope: who leads
Support for the launch, the first three questions customers will ask with their
answers, known issues, and where tickets escalate. Don't accept "Support will
figure it out". Also, success metrics must come from docs/metrics-catalog.md with
the owner it names, and a metric that isn't there becomes an open question.
```

You do not need to know that John's PRD runs through `bmad-facilitate`. `bmad-customize` finds the `prd` template, decides this is an extension because you are adding to the PRD rather than rebuilding it, and shows you a file like this before writing it:

```markdown
---
extends: prd
---

## Support readiness
<!-- After MVP scope. What Support needs on launch day. Ask who leads Support for this launch, then ask the user to picture the first week of tickets: the three questions customers will ask first, and the answer to each. Add known issues and where a ticket escalates. Push back on "Support will figure it out": a launch with no answers ready is not ready. -->

## Success metrics
<!-- Adds to the template's Success metrics. Every metric comes from `docs/metrics-catalog.md` and names the owner it lists; read the catalog before asking. When the user proposes a metric the catalog lacks, say so and log an open question for its owner instead of inventing a definition. -->
```

Each comment is a facilitation instruction:

- **Support readiness** is a new heading, so it is added to every PRD. Its comment places it ("After MVP scope"), says what to ask and in what order, and says when to push back. It is required, because the comment does not start with `optional` or `include when`.
- **Success metrics** has the same heading as a section John's PRD already has, so it changes that section. "Adds to" keeps John's own instructions for the section and adds Larkspur's. A comment that said "Replaces the template's Success metrics" would use Larkspur's alone.

Say yes, and `bmad-customize` saves it in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`, under a name such as `prd-larkspur.md`, then shows the merged PRD: Support readiness is now in the facilitation order as a required section. Commit the file so your whole team gets it.

## Step 3: Write a PRD with John

Talk to John (`bmad-agent-pm`):

```text
John, let's create a PRD for text message appointment reminders.
```

John coaches the PRD as usual, and tells you up front that your project adds rules to it. On the fast path he raises both rules in his first batch of questions; when coaching, he raises each as the conversation reaches it. When the conversation reaches Success metrics, he offers metrics from your catalog, such as no-show rate. Propose one the catalog lacks, such as "patient happiness", and he says it is not in the catalog and logs an open question for its owner instead of defining it himself. After MVP scope he asks who leads Support for the launch, then walks you through the first week of tickets. Answer "Support will figure it out" and he presses for the answers.

## Step 4: See What the Coach Read

Open the PRD's folder. Beside the PRD and its `.memlog.md` is `.template.md`: John's PRD template merged with every extension of it, the extensions first. Your file's text sits at the top, under a line naming its path.

If a rule ever seems ignored, look here first. Text that is not in `.template.md` never reached the coach.

## Step 5: When Changes Outgrow an Extension

Larkspur's billing team writes PRDs for changes to pricing, invoices and payments. Their documents need sections an ordinary PRD does not have, such as proration, tax and Finance sign-off, and skip some it does have. Adding those to the `prd` extension would put billing sections in every team's PRD. The more you change, the more a separate document makes sense:

| Changes | Use | Template id |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A few sections and rules for everyone | An extension | `extends: prd` |
| A different shape for everyone in the project | A replacement copy | `template: prd` |
| A different document for one team or kind of work | A new template | `template: prd-billing` |

Billing needs the third. Ask `bmad-customize`:

```text
The billing team needs its own PRD for changes to pricing, invoices and payments.
Start from John's PRD. Add a section that walks through what each customer pays
the day the change lands, with a worked example, and a Finance sign-off section.
Drop Users and journeys.
```

It copies John's template to `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/prd-billing.md`, gives it a new id, and adds your sections, such as:

```markdown
---
template: prd-billing
description: "Requirements for a change to pricing, invoices or payments."
not_for: "Product work that does not change what customers pay or how they are billed (`prd`)."
agents: [bmad-agent-pm]
---

## What each customer pays
<!-- After Features and requirements. Walk the user through the day the change lands: mid-cycle upgrades, downgrades, refunds and annual plans. Ask for one worked example with real numbers, and push until every case names who absorbs the difference. -->
```

Three lines in its frontmatter matter:

- **`template: prd-billing`** makes it a new document. John's `prd` stays as it was for everyone else.
- **`description` and `not_for`** are what John reads to choose. Ask him for "a PRD for the new annual discount" and he picks `prd-billing`; ask for one about a calendar feature and he picks `prd`.
- **`agents: [bmad-agent-pm]`** has John offer it. Without it, the template is still usable but no agent lists it.

Two trade-offs come with a copy. Your `prd-larkspur.md` extension extends `prd`, not `prd-billing`, so add Support readiness to the copy too if billing launches need it, or write a second extension with `extends: prd-billing`. And a copy does not receive updates to John's template, so compare it when BMad's PRD changes.

## What You've Accomplished

```text
your-project/
├── docs/
│   └── metrics-catalog.md                  # read by the coach for every PRD
├── _bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/
│   ├── prd-larkspur.md                     # extension: every PRD
│   └── prd-billing.md                      # new template: billing PRDs
└── _bmad-output/.../prd-text-reminders/
    ├── prd-text-reminders.md               # the PRD
    ├── .memlog.md                          # its decision log
    └── .template.md                        # what the coach read
```

## Quick Reference

| To | Do |
| --- | --- |
| Add a section to every PRD | A new heading in an `extends: prd` file, with a comment that places it and says what to ask |
| Change how an existing section is coached | The same heading in the extension, with a comment that adds to or replaces the template's |
| Remove a section | List the order in the extension's `facilitation_order` and leave the section out |
| Make HTML views by default for PRDs | `html_view: always` in the extension's frontmatter |
| Give one team its own document | A copy with a new `template` id, `description`, `not_for` and `agents` |
| Check what a run used | Open `.template.md` in the run folder |

## Common Questions

**Will updating BMad overwrite my changes?** No. Updates never touch `_bmad/custom/`. Your extension keeps applying, and John's improvements to the PRD still reach you through it.

**Can I write these files by hand?** Yes. [Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md) covers the format, and `bmad-customize` checks a file you wrote yourself.

**Who gets the change?** Everyone who pulls the project, since `_bmad/custom/` is committed. For a change only you want in every project, put the file in `~/.bmad/facilitate-templates/`.

**Does this work for Mary's documents too?** Yes. Extend `brief`, `prfaq` or `brd` the same way.

## Getting Help

Ask the `bmad` skill, or bring questions to the [BMad Discord](https://discord.gg/gk8jAdXWmj).

:::tip[Key Takeaways]
Templates are facilitation instructions: a section comment says where the section goes, what to ask and when to push. Extend a template by default so updates keep arriving, and copy it only to rebuild a document or to give one team a document of its own. `.template.md` shows exactly what the coach read.
:::

---
title: 'Customize BMad'
description: Change how an installed agent or workflow behaves — with bmad-customize or by hand — and know what is customizable, where an override lands, and how it merges.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

You want an agent to remember your organization's rules, a workflow to
publish its output somewhere, a menu item that runs your own skill, or a
different name on the roster. Each of these is an override file next to
BMad's installed defaults. Updates do not touch your files, and you do not
edit installed files.

## Start with the guided path

Run the `bmad-customize` skill and say what you want changed. It scans your
installation for what is customizable, picks the right surface for your
intent (an agent or a workflow), writes the override file, and verifies
that the merged result contains your change. Use it for any per-skill
change. The rest of this page describes what each surface exposes and how
the pieces combine.

It also changes the documents agents write, such as a section every PRD must have or HTML by default, by writing an extension of that document's template; you do not need to know which skill writes it. See [Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md#extend-a-template).

There are two surfaces:

| Surface | File | Shapes |
|---|---|---|
| Per-skill override | `_bmad/custom/<skill>.toml` | How one agent or workflow behaves when it activates: persona, facts, hooks, menu, workflow fields |
| Central configuration | `_bmad/custom/config.toml` | Setup answers and agent descriptors that other skills read |

`bmad-customize` writes per-skill overrides only. Central configuration is
hand-authored; see [Central configuration](#central-configuration).

For ready-made team recipes (an agent-wide rule, publishing to Confluence,
swapping a template, a rebranded roster), see
[Adopt BMad Across a Team](./adopt-bmad-across-a-team.md).

## What an agent is made of

Every named agent has two parts. Name, title, and domain are fixed:
"hey Mary" always activates the analyst. Everything else is customizable:
role, identity statement, communication style, principles, icon, menu,
persistent facts, and activation hooks. The shipped agents are listed in
[Agents](../reference/skills-and-agents.md#agents).

The per-skill file controls how the agent behaves when it activates.
Central configuration controls how `bmad-party-mode`, `bmad-retrospective`,
and `bmad-advanced-elicitation` introduce the agent. Rewriting Mary's
principles is per-skill; changing the one-line description a party uses
to introduce her is central.

:::note[Prerequisites]

- BMad installed in your project (see [Install BMad](../start/install-bmad.md)).
- [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) on your PATH. BMad runs the resolver with `uv run`, which provisions Python for you; there is nothing to `pip install`.
:::

## How overrides merge

Every customizable skill ships a `customize.toml` in its installed folder.
That file is the schema: read it to see what is customizable. Never edit
it; updates overwrite it. Instead, create sparse override files that
contain only the fields you change.

**Three layers.** The resolver reads three files and the highest wins:

```text
Priority 1 (wins): _bmad/custom/<skill>.user.toml   (personal, gitignored)
Priority 2:        _bmad/custom/<skill>.toml        (team, committed)
Priority 3 (base): the skill's own customize.toml   (shipped defaults)
```

`_bmad/custom/` starts empty. Files appear only when someone customizes.

**Four rules, by shape.** The resolver does not treat fields differently by
name; the merge depends only on the value's shape:

| Shape | Rule |
|---|---|
| Scalar (string, int, bool, float) | Override wins |
| Table | Deep merge — apply these rules recursively |
| Array of tables where every item has `code`, or every item has `id` | Merge by that key: matching keys replace in place, new keys append |
| Any other array (scalars, tables with no key, arrays mixing `code` and `id`) | Append — base items, then team, then user |

**No removal.** An override cannot delete a base item. To suppress a
default menu item, override it by `code` with a description or prompt that
does nothing; to restructure an array further, fork the skill. If you
author your own array of tables, use `code` on every item or `id` on every
item — mixing them falls back to append.

**Read-only fields.** `agent.name` and `agent.title` sit in
`customize.toml` as metadata, but the agent never reads them at runtime.
`name = "Bob"` in an override does nothing. For a differently named agent,
copy the skill folder, rename it, and ship it as a custom skill.

:::caution[Do not copy the whole `customize.toml`]
Every field you omit is inherited from the layer below. A full copy locks
in today's defaults, so the next update ships new values that your
override silently shadows.
:::

## Customize an agent

**Find the surface.** The schema is the skill's installed `customize.toml`:

```text
.claude/skills/bmad-agent-pm/customize.toml
```

The path varies by IDE — Cursor uses `.cursor/skills/`, Cline
`.cline/skills/`, and so on. Fields live directly under `[agent]`.

**Scalars.** Create `_bmad/custom/` in your project root if it does not
exist, then add `<skill>.toml` with only the fields you change. `icon`, `role`, `identity`, and `communication_style` are scalars,
so the override wins:

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-agent-pm.toml

[agent]
icon = "🏥"
role = "Drives product discovery for a regulated healthcare domain."
communication_style = "Precise, regulatory-aware, asks compliance-shaped questions early."
```

**Facts, principles, and hooks.** These four arrays append: shipped items
first, then team, then user. `persistent_facts` are static context the
agent keeps in mind all session; an entry is a literal sentence or a
`file:` reference (globs allowed) whose contents are loaded as facts.

```toml
[agent]
persistent_facts = [
  "Our org is AWS-only -- do not propose GCP or Azure.",
  "file:{project-root}/docs/compliance/hipaa-overview.md",
]

principles = [
  "Ship nothing that can't pass an FDA audit.",
]

# Runs before the greeting.
activation_steps_prepend = [
  "Scan {project-root}/docs/compliance/ and load any HIPAA-related documents as context.",
]

# Runs after the greeting, before the menu.
activation_steps_append = [
  "Read {project-root}/_bmad/custom/company-glossary.md if it exists.",
]
```

Prepend runs before the greeting, when the greeting itself needs that
context. Append runs after, for setup the user should not wait on.

**Menu.** `[[agent.menu]]` is an array of tables keyed by `code`, so a
matching code replaces the shipped item and a new code appends. Each item
has exactly one of `skill` or `prompt`:

```toml
# Replace the shipped VALIDATE item with your own skill
[[agent.menu]]
code = "VALIDATE"
description = "Review a planning document against our delivery standards"
skill = "custom-validate-plan"

# Add a new item
[[agent.menu]]
code = "COMPLIANCE"
description = "Run compliance pre-check"
prompt = """
Read {project-root}/_bmad/custom/compliance-checklist.md
and scan all documents in {output_folder}/{active_initiative} against it.
"""
```

When any field points at a file, spell out the full path from
`{project-root}`, even for a file sitting next to your override in
`_bmad/custom/`. The agent resolves `{project-root}` at runtime.

**Team or personal.** The team file (`bmad-agent-pm.toml`) is committed
and shared: compliance rules, company persona, custom menu items. The
personal file (`bmad-agent-pm.user.toml`) is gitignored: tone, private
preferences, facts only you want the agent to hold.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-agent-pm.user.toml

[agent]
persistent_facts = [
  "Always include a rough complexity estimate (low/medium/high) when presenting options.",
]
```

## Customize a workflow

Workflows — skills that drive a multi-step process, such as
`bmad-facilitate` — use the same files and rules. Their surface lives
under `[workflow]`. The baseline fields every customizable workflow
exposes are the same hooks and facts as agents plus `on_complete`. For
workflows, a `persistent_facts` entry is a literal sentence, a `file:`
path or glob, or a `skill:` reference to a skill that holds relevant
knowledge. `on_complete` is a string, or an array of instructions run in
order, that runs once the workflow finishes its main output:

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]
activation_steps_prepend = [
  "Load {project-root}/docs/product/north-star-principles.md as context.",
]

persistent_facts = [
  "Every planning document names its regulatory risks.",
  "file:{project-root}/docs/compliance/document-checklist.md",
]

on_complete = "Summarize the document in three bullets and offer to email it via the gws-gmail-send skill."
```

Individual workflows add fields on top — output paths, templates, toggles —
and each follows the shape rules above. For example, `bmad-build`,
`bmad-build-auto`, and `bmad-code-review` each expose `review`, the default
review depth. The build skills default to `quick` and code review to
`thorough`; this raises every build's review to four lenses:

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-build.toml
[workflow]
review = "thorough"
```

Read a workflow's `customize.toml` to see the fields it exposes. If the
field you need is not there, use `activation_steps_*` and
`persistent_facts`, or open an issue asking for a customization point.

**Activation order.** A customizable workflow activates in a fixed
sequence, so you know when each hook fires:

1. Resolve the `[workflow]` block (base, then team, then user).
2. Run `activation_steps_prepend`.
3. Load `persistent_facts` as context for the run.
4. Load config and resolve standard variables (project name, languages, paths, date).
5. Greet the user.
6. Run `activation_steps_append`.

The workflow body begins after step 6.

## Override one rendered invocation

To change a skill's customization for one run only, add `--set key=value`
arguments or an `--overrides <file.toml>` file to the `render_skill.py`
command in its `SKILL.md`. Persistent project and user files stay as they
are.

```bash
uv run /abs/project/_bmad/scripts/render_skill.py \
  --project-root /abs/project \
  --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-build \
  --overrides ./invocation.toml \
  --set 'workflow.on_complete=Summarize the result in three bullets.'
```

Keys are dotted parameter paths such as `workflow.on_complete`. The
override file has the same shape as the skill's `customize.toml`. Both
layer on top of the persistent files, and `--set` wins over the file.

String values can be written as plain text. Other types use TOML syntax:

```bash
--set 'workflow.persistent_facts=["Additional context"]'
```

## Central configuration

Per-skill files cover one agent or workflow. Setup answers and agent
overrides live in three TOML files:

```text
_bmad/config.toml               (setup-owned)     team scope: setup answers
_bmad/custom/config.toml        (human-authored)  team overrides (committed)
_bmad/custom/config.user.toml   (human-authored)  personal overrides (gitignored), including `[core] active_initiative`
```

**Three layers**, merged with the same shape rules:

```text
Priority 1 (wins): _bmad/custom/config.user.toml
Priority 2:        _bmad/custom/config.toml
Priority 3 (base): _bmad/config.toml
```

**What lives where.** `bmad setup` writes the `[modules.<code>]` answers a
module's setup questions produce, plus the `[core]` defaults. A question with
scope `team` lands in `_bmad/config.toml`; a question with scope `user` is
stored in `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml`. `[agents.<code>]` tables are
optional: the roster comes from each module's `roster.toml`, and a table in
either `_bmad/custom/` file applies on top.

**Editing rules.** `bmad setup` fills in missing keys in `_bmad/config.toml`
and never changes an existing value. To change an answer, edit its
`modules.<code>.<key>` value in the file that holds it, or ask `bmad` to
change it. To pin a value for the whole team, set it in
`_bmad/custom/config.toml`. Setup adds user-scope answers to
`_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` and moves the files of renamed skills, but
never changes a value already in either `_bmad/custom/` file. Both files are
the place for custom agents, descriptor overrides, and pinned values.

**Rebrand an agent.** Party mode and other roster skills pick up the new
description automatically:

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.toml

[agents.bmad-agent-pm]
description = "Healthcare PM — regulatory-aware, stakeholder-driven, FDA-shaped questions first."
```

**Add a fictional agent.** No skill folder is needed; the descriptor alone
lets a party include Kirk, and the `team` field filters who gets invited.
See [Run Multi-Agent Discussions](./run-multi-agent-discussions.md).

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.user.toml

[agents.kirk]
team = "startrek"
name = "Captain James T. Kirk"
title = "Starship Captain"
icon = "🖖"
description = "Bold, rule-bending commander. Speaks in dramatic pauses."
```

**Override a setup answer.** The override wins over `_bmad/config.toml`; a
developer's own `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` still wins over it:

```toml
# _bmad/custom/config.toml

[core]
output_folder = "/shared/org-bmad-output"
```

**Which surface to use:**

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Add MCP tool calls to every dev workflow | Per-skill: `_bmad/custom/bmad-agent-dev.toml` `persistent_facts` |
| Add a menu item to an agent | Per-skill: `_bmad/custom/bmad-agent-<role>.toml` `[[agent.menu]]` |
| Swap a workflow's output template | Per-skill: `_bmad/custom/<workflow>.toml` scalar override |
| Add, replace or extend a `bmad-facilitate` template, including John's planning templates | A template file in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`; see [Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md) |
| Rebrand an agent's public descriptor | Central: `_bmad/custom/config.toml` `[agents.<code>]` |
| Add a custom or fictional agent to the roster | Central: `_bmad/custom/config.*.toml` new `[agents.<code>]` |
| Set shared team defaults | Central: `_bmad/custom/config.toml` `[modules.<code>]` or `[core]` |
| Choose which initiative your documents and tickets go to | Central: `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` `[core] active_initiative`, or ask the `bmad` skill to switch it |

## Check what resolved

On activation, a shared Python script merges the files and returns the
result as JSON. Run it yourself to see exactly what an agent or workflow
will use:

```bash
# Resolve the full agent block
uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \
  --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-agent-pm \
  --project-root {project-root} \
  --key agent

# Resolve a single field
uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \
  --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-agent-pm \
  --project-root {project-root} \
  --key agent.icon

# Full dump: omit --key
```

Replace `{project-root}` with your project root; the skill resolves it
for you at activation, but a shell will not.

`--skill` points at the skill's installed directory; the script derives
the skill name from that folder and finds the matching `_bmad/custom/`
files itself. Output is always JSON.

`--project-root` names the project whose `_bmad/custom/` files apply.
Skills pass it on activation. Omit it and the script infers a root —
working directory first, then its own install path, then the skill
directory — which lands correctly in ordinary use but has to guess when a
skill is installed under your home directory and a `~/_bmad` exists there
too. If it picks a root with no override for that skill while another
candidate has one, it says so on stderr rather than quietly returning
defaults.

Use `uv run` so the script gets Python 3.11 or later. If you run it with
`python3` instead, check the version: 3.10 and earlier lack `tomllib`.
If the script cannot run, an agent reads the three TOML files and applies
the same rules; many workflows fall back to shipped defaults, so keep `uv`
working if you rely on workflow overrides.

## Troubleshooting

**Customization not appearing.** Check that the file is in `_bmad/custom/`
and named exactly after the skill directory. Check TOML syntax: strings
quoted, `[section]` for tables, `[[section]]` for arrays of tables, and a
table's scalar or array keys placed before any of its `[[subtables]]`. For
agents, fields belong under `[agent]`. Remember that `agent.name` and
`agent.title` are read-only.

**An update broke it.** You probably copied the full `customize.toml`.
Trim the override back to only the fields you changed.

**See what is customizable.** Run `bmad-customize`, which lists every
customizable skill and which already have overrides, or read the skill's
`customize.toml` directly.

**Reset.** Delete the override file from `_bmad/custom/`. The skill falls
back to its shipped defaults.
docs/customize/how-document-templates-wo:
---
title: 'How Document Templates Work'
description: Where the documents John, Mary and bmad-facilitate write come from, and the three ways a team changes one.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

Every document John (`bmad-agent-pm`) and Mary (`bmad-agent-analyst`) write runs through one skill, `bmad-facilitate`, and one markdown template per document type. The template is the whole definition of the document: its sections, what the coach asks for each one, when it pushes back, and what the review checks. To change a document, you change its template, never the skill.

## A Template Is Facilitation Instructions

A template's headings are the document's sections. Its comments tell the coach how to work:

| Comment | Says |
| --- | --- |
| `purpose`, `stance` | What the document is for and how the coach behaves, such as "a challenge, not a write-up" |
| `inputs` | What only the user knows, so it is always asked and never guessed |
| `writing`, `done when` | Rules for the text, and the test that ends the questioning |
| Under a heading | Where the section goes, what to ask, when to press, and whether it is required |

The user never sees the template. They have a conversation, and the comments shape it.

## Where Templates Come From

The skill searches these places in order, and for each id the first template found wins:

1. Your project's `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/` folder, committed so the whole team gets it.
2. Your personal `~/.bmad/facilitate-templates/` folder, for every project you work in.
3. Any other library your team adds to `template_libraries`, such as a folder or GitHub repository your organization keeps.
4. The agent's own templates, such as John's PRD.
5. Each installed module's `doc-templates/` folder.

## Three Ways to Change a Document

| You want | Do this | Updates to the original |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The same document with your rules: a section added, one replaced or removed, a question always asked, HTML by default | An **extension**: a file with `extends: prd` holding only your changes | Still arrive |
| The same document rebuilt for everyone in the project | A **replacement**: a copy with the same id, `template: prd` | Stop |
| A different document beside the original, such as a PRD for one department | A **new template**: a copy with a new id, `template: prd-billing` | Stop |

Start with an extension. Move to a copy only when your changes outgrow it, because a copy no longer receives the fixes and improvements to the template it came from. The test is how much of the original you still want: if most of it, extend; if your team needs a different shape, make a new template and leave the original for everyone else.

## What a Run Reads

When a run starts, the skill merges the template and every extension of it into one file and works from that file alone, the extensions first so their rules win. It saves the file as `.template.md` in the run folder, beside the document, so you can always see exactly what the coach read.

Settings that cover every document, such as doc standards, reviewers, where output goes and whether HTML views are made, live in `_bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml` instead of a template.

You do not need to know any of this to make a change. Tell `bmad-customize` what you want, such as "every PRD needs a support readiness section", and it decides between an extension, a copy and a setting, writes the file and shows you the merged result. [Customize a Document for Your Team](./customize-a-document-for-your-team.md) walks through all three ways with a real example, [Write a Document Template](./write-a-document-template.md) covers the file format in full, and [Document Templates](../reference/document-templates.md) lists the shipped templates.
docs/customize/run-multi-agent-discussio:
---
title: 'Run Multi-Agent Discussions'
description: Put your BMad agents in one conversation, choose how independently they think, build a custom cast, and use the two shipped parties.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

`bmad-party-mode` puts your installed BMad agents in one conversation, in
character, with you steering.

## What a party is

Run `/bmad-party-mode` and the agents your installed modules provide join
the same conversation: the PM, Architect, Dev, UX Designer, and the rest.
They answer in character, agree, disagree, and build on each other. You
steer: ask a follow-up, push back, bring one voice forward, or change the
subject.

Each agent brings a different priority — design, scope, what is buildable —
so the tradeoff is visible now.

**Good for:**

- Decisions with real tradeoffs
- Brainstorming and "what are we missing?"
- Post-mortems and retrospectives
- Pressure-testing a plan before you commit

You can start a party from inside any other workflow.

:::note[Example]
**You:** Monolith or microservices for the MVP?

**Architect:** Start monolith. Microservices add operating cost you don't need at a thousand users.

**PM:** Agreed. Time to market matters more than scaling we can't prove yet.

**Dev:** Monolith, but with clean module boundaries so we can split a service out later without a rewrite.
:::

## Start a party

Invoke the skill and say what you want; it works out whether you mean to run
or build one.

| Goal | Type this |
| --- | --- |
| Start a party in the default mode | `/bmad-party-mode` |
| Start in a specific mode | `/bmad-party-mode --mode auto` (also `session`, `subagent`, `agent-team`) |
| Run it once, non-interactively | `/bmad-party-mode --non-interactive "review this PR"` |
| Open a saved party | `/bmad-party-mode --party code-review-crew` |
| See the saved parties | `/bmad-party-mode --list-groups` |
| Create a cast on the spot | "party mode with the bridge crew of the Enterprise" |
| Create or edit a party | "party mode, create a new party" or "party mode, edit the writers' room" |
| Set the skill's defaults | `/bmad-customize bmad-party-mode` |

## Choose a mode

One mode is active per session. It decides who does the thinking: one model
voicing everyone, or separate agents reasoning on their own.

| Mode | What it does | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session` | Default. One model voices every persona inline. | Most conversations: banter, brainstorming, quick back-and-forth. |
| `auto` | Voices inline for light rounds, spawns independent agents only when independence changes the answer. | You want speed most of the time and real independence on the hard rounds. |
| `subagent` | Spawns a separate agent for each persona every substantive round. | Reviews and focus groups, where the voices must stay independent. |
| `agent-team` | Runs the personas as a persistent team whose members address each other directly. Claude Code only. | A live, hands-off round-table where the agents talk among themselves. |

One model voicing five personas tends to make them agree. Separate agents
keep their reasoning independent, which is the point of a review panel or a
focus group, at a higher cost. `auto` spawns independent agents only when a
round needs it.

When your tool can't run the mode you asked for, the party falls back:
`agent-team` drops to `subagent`, then to `session`. The configured default
lives in your customization; a runtime `--mode` flag wins for that session.

A party is interactive by default: the opening ask is a starting topic, and
the room stays open until you end it. To serve one intent and stop, start
with `--non-interactive`; the party runs to a natural close, wraps up, and
releases any spawned agents.

## Build your own party

You can also build a cast from any personas you describe and save it to
reuse. The same skill writes the result through
[bmad-customize](./customize-bmad.md). Two ideas do most of the work.

**Personas** make a member unmistakable: how they talk, what they value, how
they argue. "Skeptical CFO" is a placeholder. "Won't approve anything without
a payback under eighteen months, and says so first" is a persona.

**Scenes** set the stage in one freeform line: the setting, what is
happening, who is hostile to whom, who pushes hardest. Define a member once
and drop them into different rooms.

| Shape | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Themed cast | Famous investors, a TV ensemble — distinct voices around a topic. |
| One-off personas | A persona or two added to the pool, no group needed. |
| Focus group from data | Hand it customer or survey data; it builds representative personas. Pair with `subagent` so the customers stay independent. |
| Review panel | Critical lenses that argue about what matters. The Code Review Crew is one. |
| Deliberation scaffold | A room that makes you think harder without pretending to decide for you. The Anti-Consensus Club is one. |
| Open-cast room | No fixed roster. The scene names a universe and the room is cast on the fly. |

Run `/bmad-customize bmad-party-mode` to pin a saved group as the default
party, choose its starting mode, and set house rules for the whole session.

Any set of voices becomes a party: a founder squad, a compliance team, the
authors of the Agile Manifesto, a room of comedians.

## The Code Review Crew

The Code Review Crew ships alongside the default party as a template to
study before you build your own: five viewpoints on a change that argue
about what matters.

| Member | Lens |
| --- | --- |
| Vex | Security — threat-models everything and names the concrete exploit path. |
| Grumbal | The adversary — assumes the code is broken and sets out to prove it. |
| Boundary | Edge cases — every branch, null, race, oversized input, odd timezone. |
| Yui | The craftsman — simplicity, naming, no needless cleverness or duplication. |
| Dana | The pragmatist — counters the perfectionists and ranks what's real versus a nit. |

The crew ships inactive: the members sit in the pool and never join the
default room. Open it with `--party code-review-crew` and `--mode subagent`
so each viewpoint reviews on its own before they discuss.

:::note[A debate, not a review]
The crew argues. It does not verify or triage. For a review that produces
verified, ranked findings, use [Review a Change](../build/review-a-change.md).
:::

## The Anti-Consensus Club

The Anti-Consensus Club helps with decisions and fuzzy questions where one
assistant might agree too quickly or keep debating after the useful work is
done. It is not a voting body: it raises objections, checks claims, stops
repetition, and returns the decision to you.

| Member | Lens |
| --- | --- |
| Wildcard | Option generator — suggests alternative problem statements, assumptions, and examples. |
| Level | Claim checker — checks support, missing information, and confidence. |
| Killjoy | Loop stopper — stops repetition, fake disagreement, and unsupported speculation. |
| Splinter | Consensus challenger — questions easy agreement and ignored tradeoffs. |

Run it as `/bmad-party-mode --party anti-consensus-club --mode subagent`. The
room recommends that mode at session start, then stops asking if you
continue in another.

## Steer the room

- Bring someone in: "Bring in the UX designer."
- Go deep on one voice: "Winston, take that apart."
- Switch rooms mid-session: "Switch to the writers' room" swaps the active group and carries the thread over.
- Summon anyone by name, even a custom member who isn't in the current room.

In every mode the result reads as one conversation and the personas stay in
character.

## Memory

A party with memory keeps a record of past sessions — the dynamics between
members, open threads, where things landed — and picks up there next time.
It is not a transcript: it keeps the few things worth remembering, without
breaking character.

In a remembered party, someone who joined from an open-cast scene or a
member you add mid-conversation is kept too; at wrap-up the room offers to
save them into the roster. The default installed-agent room remembers unless
you turn it off in `/bmad-customize bmad-party-mode`. Both shipped parties
and any cast you create inline start fresh each time; save a cast as a party
and choose memory to give it one.

## A keepsake of the session

When you wrap up, the party offers a keepsake: one self-contained HTML
document of the session, laid out by persona, written as
`party-<slug>/party-<slug>.html` in the active initiative's folder, or in the
output folder when none is active. Decline it and the party ends.
docs/customize/write-a-document-template:
---
title: 'Write a Document Template'
description: Add your own template to bmad-facilitate, replace or hide a shipped one, add your team's rules to a template, and set how rendered views look.
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

Use the `bmad-facilitate` template library to make the skill coach your team through your own document types. Everything about a document is data. Template files say what each document asks for and what the review checks. The skill's customization says where templates live, where the result goes, and how the HTML view looks.

New to templates? [How Document Templates Work](./how-document-templates-work.md) explains the pieces, and [Customize a Document for Your Team](./customize-a-document-for-your-team.md) walks through changing a shipped one. This page is the full guide to the file format.

## When to use this

- Your team has a document type the shipped templates do not cover.
- Your organization has its own format for a postmortem, a proposal, or a decision record.
- A shipped template is right, but your team has rules to add: a policy to cite, a section it must contain, a check for the review.
- Rendered views should carry your team's look.

:::note[Prerequisites]
BMad installed with the core tools, and `bmad setup` run. Templates go in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`. Settings go in `_bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml`, which the team commits; `bmad-facilitate.user.toml` beside it holds personal changes. `bmad-customize` writes any of these for you, an extension of a shipped template included: tell it what to change, such as "every PRD opens with a quote". How overrides merge is in [Customize BMad](./customize-bmad.md).
:::

## Add a template to the library

Save the template in `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`, with any rubric or method catalog beside it. The skill lists every markdown file there whose frontmatter has `template:`. Nothing else needs registering.

```yaml
---
title: ""
template: runbook
version: 1.0.0
description: "Step-by-step instructions for one alert or recurring task."
rubric: rubric-runbook.md
status: draft
created: ""
updated: ""
---
```

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `template` | Kebab-case id. It names the run folder, and a later update uses it to find the template. |
| `version` | Optional version of the template. It is copied into each document, so a later update can say the template has moved on. |
| `description` | One short line saying what the template is for. Help lists it for every template on every run, so keep it under about 80 characters. Quote it, because a colon breaks unquoted YAML. |
| `not_for` | Optional short line naming what the template is not for, and the template to use instead. Read with `description` when choosing one, and not listed in help. |
| `paced` | Optional. `true` walks the sections in order, one at a time, for a document whose conversation matters as much as the result. See [Walk the sections in order](#walk-the-sections-in-order). |
| `facilitation_order` | The sections by id, in the order the skill takes them up, with `?` on each one that is not required. See [Order the sections](#order-the-sections). |
| `guidance` | Optional rules shared by a family of templates and read as part of each, as a path relative to the template, or the bare name `guidance-planning` for the shipped planning rules: stakes from hobby to regulated, `[ASSUMPTION]` tags in the body, stable ids and testable requirements, and detail pushed to the level below. Every shipped template sets it. Without it the skill names no stakes levels and tags nothing in the body; a document such as fiction says what it needs in its own comments. |
| `agents` | Optional list of the skills that run this template, such as `[bmad-agent-pm]`. The `bmad` skill uses it to say who offers the template. A template in an agent's `assets/` folder counts as that agent's without it. |
| `rubric` | Optional path to a rubric for the review, relative to the template, or the bare name `rubric-planning` for the shipped planning rubric. Empty uses the shipped general rubric, which suits any document. |
| `methods` | Optional path to a method catalog, relative to the template: a CSV whose rows supply the questions the coaching asks. |
| `output` | Optional run folder for this template. It may use `{output_folder}`, `{active_initiative}`, `{id}` and `{slug}`. |
| `style` | Optional CSS file for this template's rendered view, relative to the template. |
| `view` | Optional layout for the rendered view: `document`, `slides`, or an HTML file relative to the template. It says what the view looks like, not whether it is made. See [Give a template its own view](#give-a-template-its-own-view). |
| `html_view` | Optional. Whether this template's view is made: `always`, `offer` or `never`, replacing the team's setting for this template. Set `always` when the view is the deliverable, as `pitch-deck` does for its slides. A team's `never` still stops it. |

`template`, `version` and `view` stay in the finished document, as does any field you add for a view to show. The other fields stay out.

A method catalog has the header `category,method,name,description,key_questions`, with the key questions separated by `|`. The shipped `security-review` template uses one for the OWASP Top 10 and STRIDE:

```csv
category,method,name,description,key_questions
release,rollback,Rollback,How a change is undone.,"How is this change undone?|Who can run the rollback?"
```

## Replace a shipped template

The first template with an id wins, and installed modules' templates are searched last, so a template in any library with the same `template:` value replaces one a module installed. To change an installed template, copy it from the module's `doc-templates/` folder into yours, with any rubric or catalog it names, keep its `template:` value and edit the copy. To use your organization's postmortem format, save it in your folder with `template: postmortem`.

## Use more than one library

`template_libraries` lists where templates live, in search order. It starts with your project's `_bmad/custom/facilitate-templates/`, then `~/.bmad/facilitate-templates/` for personal templates you want in every project. An override appends to the list, and a folder that is missing or empty adds nothing.

```toml
# _bmad/custom/bmad-facilitate.toml

[workflow]
template_libraries = ["https://github.com/fernhollow/doc-templates@v1.2.0"]
```

| Entry | Example |
| --- | --- |
| A folder or one template file | `{project-root}/docs/templates` or `~/templates` |
| A GitHub repo, folder or file, read through `gh` | `https://github.com/fernhollow/doc-templates/tree/v1.2.0/planning` |
| A URL to one `.md` file | `https://example.com/templates/runbook.md` |
| A sentence naming the tool that reaches it | `Search corp:confluence_search in the DOCS space for templates` |

A library you cannot share goes in `bmad-facilitate.user.toml`, which stays out of git. A teammate without access who updates one of those documents follows its existing headings instead. If a library cannot be read, the skill names it and carries on with the others.

:::caution[Trust]
A template overrides the skill, so a remote library can direct an agent that has tools. Point only at sources you control. A branch or tag can move, so pin a commit SHA with `@ref` when the library must not change between runs.
:::

## Ship templates in a module

A module adds templates by putting them in `doc-templates/` in its record folder, the folder holding its `bmod.toml`, with any rubric or catalog beside them. They are offered once the module is installed, with no setting, and they update with the module. The shipped templates live this way in `bmod-method`, `bmad-founder-agent-advisor` and `bmod-cis`.

An organization can keep its templates in its own modules, one per program if it likes, such as `bmod-fernhollow-cards`. A module should add new ids or extend existing ones, because an extension applies wherever it sits. To replace an id outright, use a project's folder, which is searched first.

## Write the template file

A template is a markdown file in three parts: the document's frontmatter, comments that guide the coaching, and its sections. Frontmatter comes first. The comments never appear in the finished document. Where a template and the skill disagree, the template wins, on every path; only a headless run still asks nothing.

```markdown
---
title: ""
template: runbook
version: 1.0.0
description: "Step-by-step instructions for one alert or recurring task."
facilitation_order: [when-to-use, severity, steps, rollback?, escalation?]
status: draft
created: ""
updated: ""
---

<!-- purpose: Let an on-call operator handle one alert or task without help. -->

<!-- stance: Walk the procedure as the operator would and ask what they check after each step. -->

<!-- inputs: The alert or task, the access it needs, the exact commands. Only the user knows the failures they have seen. -->

<!-- writing:
  - Numbered steps, one action each, with its expected result.
  - Commands copied exactly.
-->

<!-- done when: Someone new to the system can follow it alone and knows when to escalate. -->

# {title}

## When to use
<!-- The alert, symptom or schedule that starts this runbook. -->

## Severity
<!-- The user must pick exactly one of: sev1, sev2, sev3. -->

## Steps
<!-- Numbered actions with expected results. When a step says "check the dashboard", ask which one and what a good reading is. diagram: flowchart -->

## Rollback
<!-- include when: a step changes production. How to undo each change. -->

## Escalation
<!-- optional. Who to call and when. -->
```

Above the first heading, give each of these keys its own comment, a line or two. All are optional:

| Key | What it tells the skill |
| --- | --- |
| `purpose` | The decision or job the document serves. |
| `stance` | How to coach for this document, including how a path should run. |
| `inputs` | What must be asked, and which of it only the user knows. Each one is asked on the coaching and fast paths unless the user already gave it, so list only what you want asked. |
| `writing` | Rules specific to this document. |
| `companions` | Other files to write beside the document, when, and what each holds. A file for a different reader belongs here, not overflow from the document. |
| `done when` | The test that ends the questioning. |
| `view` | The brief for an HTML page written for each document. See [Give a template its own view](#give-a-template-its-own-view). |
| `next` | What to offer or do once the document is done, such as handing it to a build. |

Add `view: slides` to the frontmatter for a slide view, or name an HTML view file; without it the HTML view is one page. In the document body, `{title}` is the only placeholder.

Each section has one comment: a line on what goes in the section, then `diagram:` and a Mermaid kind when a picture carries the meaning (flowchart, sequence, state, timeline, gantt, er, mindmap, quadrant, journey). A section that is not required starts its comment with `optional` or `include when:` and a condition.

### Order the sections

`facilitation_order` lists every `##` section by id: its heading in lowercase, with punctuation dropped and spaces as hyphens, so `What makes it different` is `what-makes-it-different` and `What's next?` is `whats-next`. It sets the order the skill takes the sections up in, not the document's order, so an executive summary can sit first in the document and come up last. A `?` after an id marks a section that is not required.

The skill settles every section before it finishes, on every path. A required section is always filled. An optional one is offered when the order reaches it, and the user decides. An include-when one is checked against its condition, and the skill says what it found. The fast path settles them too, so asking for speed never drops a section quietly. Sections left out are named at the end with the reason.

The template list reports an id that names no heading, an id listed twice, and a heading left off the list. Every shipped template sets the key. A template without it still works: a section whose comment does not start with `optional` or `include when:` is required, and the document's order is the order.

Say what goes in each section, not how to write well. Leave out example content, which the model would copy.

A section comment can also steer the conversation or limit the answer, in plain sentences. The `Steps` comment above tells the skill when to press, and `Severity` limits the user to a list. A list can live elsewhere: "The user must pick a team from `docs/teams.md`." The shipped `decision-record` and `security-review` templates show both, and [Document Templates](../reference/document-templates.md) lists where to see each capability.

### Walk the sections in order

Set `paced: true` when going through the sections is the point, as in a PRFAQ, where the user defends each part before moving on. The skill shows the sections in facilitation order before it starts, then takes them one at a time and finishes each before opening the next.

In a paced template, each section comment is the brief for that part of the session. A voice, stance or method it sets, such as "you are now a skeptical customer", replaces the skill's coaching defaults until the section closes, so write it as instructions to the coach rather than only a description of the content. These shipped templates are paced: Mary's `prfaq` and `brief`, John's `experiment`, `opportunity` and `pitch`, and the module's `decision-record` and `postmortem`.

Every run shows a progress line on the messages that ask something: `PRFAQ · Customer FAQ (2 of 4)` when paced, `PRD · 6 of 24 done` otherwise. The total is every section in the facilitation order, and a section counts once it is settled, so the total stays the same for the whole run.

Put a bare `## Table of Contents` heading right after the title of any template whose documents run long. Agents often read only the top of a file to judge it, so the skill fills this with a linked entry per section and a short phrase of its key terms, then checks it against the final headings. It gets no slide in a slide view.

## Use a format you already have

A file with no comments is followed as written: every heading is required, in order. Save your organization's existing format in the folder with `template` and `description` in its frontmatter and it works.

```markdown
---
title: ""
template: design-note
version: 1.0.0
description: "Recording the design of a change before building it."
status: draft
---

# {title}

## Background

## Proposal

## Rollout plan

## Risks
```

Add the comments when you want the coaching, the optional sections, or the diagrams.

## Extend a template

An extension changes a template without copying it, so updates to the original still reach you. On every run the skill merges the template and its extensions into one file, the extensions first, and works from that file. It saves that file as `.template.md` in the run folder, so you can see exactly what the skill read. Save a file with `extends:` and the template's id in any library or module, and every run of that template includes it. Fernhollow Bank, a fictional company, uses the `proposal` template as it is, but every proposal must name an approval track from a fixed list and leave room for reviewers:

```markdown
---
extends: proposal
---

## Approval Track
<!-- After Budget. The user must pick exactly one of: fast-track, standard, regulated. -->

## Review Comments
<!-- Last. Keep the line below as it is; reviewers fill this in later. -->

_Reviewer comments go here._
```

An extension can hold anything a template can:

| In the extension | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| A section | Added where its comment says, and taken up at that point in the conversation. If the heading it names is gone, the skill places it by judgment. It is required unless its comment starts `optional` or `include when`, the same rule as a template's sections. With the same heading as a template section, it replaces that section or adds to it, as its comment says. |
| `facilitation_order` frontmatter | Replaces the template's whole order. A template section it leaves out is removed from the document, and the template list names it under `removed`. Set it only to reorder or remove the template's sections, never just to place a new one, because a section the template adds in a later update is also left out and removed. |
| `stance`, `inputs`, `writing` or `done when` comments | Added to the template's, and they win where they disagree with it. A policy to load goes in `inputs`; a review rule goes in `done when`. |
| `description`, `not_for`, `guidance`, `rubric`, `methods`, `output`, `style`, `view` or `html_view` frontmatter | Replaces the template's value. |

This extension opens every PRD with a quote and always makes its HTML view, while John's updates to the PRD still arrive:

```markdown
---
extends: prd
html_view: always
---

## Quote
<!-- First, right under the title. Ask the user for a quote unique to this product before anything else. -->
```

When extensions conflict, the first in search order wins. Use a copy only to rebuild a template, or with a new id for a different document; [Customize a Document for Your Team](./customize-a-document-for-your-team.md#step-5-when-changes-outgrow-an-extension) shows when.

Rules for every document, whatever the template, go in `persistent_facts`, `doc_standards` and `finalize_reviewers` under `[workflow]` instead.

## Set the look of rendered views

At close the skill can render the document as one HTML file, diagrams included. The page loads its Markdown and diagram renderers from jsDelivr when opened, so a reader with no network sees the plain text instead. Raw HTML in the document shows as text, and script links are dropped.

```toml
[workflow]
style = "{project-root}/_bmad/style/brand.css"
html_view = "always"
```

`style` is a CSS file applied to every view after the default styles; empty uses the default. A written voice or style guide belongs in `doc_standards` or a template's `writing` comment instead. A template's `style` overrides it for that template. `html_view` is `offer` (the default: ask at close), `always`, or `never`. A template's own `html_view` replaces it for that template, except that `never` here stops every view.

## Give a template its own view

A template stays markdown, and so does the document the skill writes, because the skill grows it section by section, reviews it and diffs it. An HTML result is a separate step at close, and all its instructions stay in the template. Choose how much freedom the page gets:

| You want | In the template | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The same layout every time, such as a form headed for PDF | `view: invoice.html` | A script fills the file's slots. Nothing is interpreted. |
| A shared structure that adapts to each document | `view: character-sheet.html` and a `view` comment | A subagent uses the file as a starter and follows the comment. |
| A page invented for each document, with no template | A `view` comment alone | A subagent writes it from the comment. |

The `view` comment sits above the first heading with the other comments, and says what the page should do:

```markdown
<!-- view: The sheet is the deliverable. `character-sheet.html` is a starter: keep to one printable page, and let this character's world set the look. -->
```

A written page comes only from the document, so it adds no claim the document does not hold. Each one costs a fresh generation, so the skill offers it at close unless the template sets `html_view: always` or the comment calls it the deliverable. Use the script for anything regulated or signed, where the page must not vary. `html_view = "never"` stops all three.

### Slots for a filled view

The view file is ordinary HTML with its CSS inline. Attributes mark where the document's content goes:

| Attribute | Filled with |
| --- | --- |
| `data-section="Heading"` | That `##` section, rendered. Matching ignores case. |
